### 4.3 Bounds on $\left\langle{GAGA}\right\rangle$

#### Lemma 4.3.

Suppose $M$ is a traceless matrix with $\|M\|\prec 1$ . For $A_{1},A_{2}\in\mathbb{M}_{k}^{\circ}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle| \displaystyle\prec 1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}, \displaystyle|\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle| \displaystyle\prec\rho_{1}\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}\right), \displaystyle|\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle| \displaystyle\prec\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}\right). $$

#### Proof.

We prove the first inequality here. The other two are proved similarly. See Remark 3.4 for details.

The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma 3.5. The only difference is the size of the error terms.

Similarly to (3.42), we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle \displaystyle=m_{1}m_{2}\left\langle{A_{1}A_{2}}\right\rangle+m_{1}\left\langle{A_{1}(G_{2}-m_{2}I)A_{2}}\right\rangle-m_{1}\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}}\right\rangle \displaystyle+\frac{m_{1}}{N}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle+m_{1}\left\langle{G_{1}-m_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle \displaystyle+\frac{m_{1}}{N}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}^{\circ}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{2}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle+m_{1}\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle. $$

Now we plug in $A_{2}=N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}$ into the identity above and get a system of equations.

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}\right\rangle \displaystyle=m_{1}m_{2}\left\langle{A_{1}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}\right\rangle+m_{1}\left\langle{A_{1}(G_{2}-m_{2}I)N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}\right\rangle \displaystyle-m_{1}\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}}\right\rangle+m_{1}\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}\right\rangle \displaystyle+\frac{m_{1}}{N}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle \displaystyle+\sum_{\mu}C_{\nu\mu}\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}^{\circ}}\right\rangle, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle C_{\nu\mu} \displaystyle=m_{1}\left\langle{G_{1}-m_{1}}\right\rangle\delta_{\nu\mu}+m_{1}\frac{1}{N}\left\langle{G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}_{\mu}}}\right\rangle \displaystyle=m_{1}m_{2}\left(S_{\nu\mu}-\frac{1}{N}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{N^{3/2}\eta_{*}^{1/2}}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{N\eta_{1}}\right)\delta_{\nu\mu}. $$

To bound the error terms in (4.12) we need the following lemma.

#### Lemma 4.4.

If $A\in\mathbb{M}_{k}^{\circ}$ and $B\in\mathbb{M}_{l}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle|\langle G_{1}AG_{2}B\rangle|\prec\Lambda_{k}\Lambda_{l}+\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}},\, \displaystyle|\langle\Im G_{1}AG_{2}B\rangle|\prec\rho_{1}\Lambda_{k}\Lambda_{l}+\rho_{1}\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\rho_{1}\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}, \displaystyle|\langle\Im G_{1}A\Im G_{2}B\rangle|\prec\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k}\Lambda_{l}+\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta^{*}}}+\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}. $$

Furthermore, for $B=N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\nu}^{\circ}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\langle G_{1}AG_{2}B\rangle|\prec\Lambda_{k}+\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}},\, \displaystyle|\langle\Im G_{1}AG_{2}B\rangle|\prec\rho_{1}\Lambda_{k}+\rho_{1}\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}, \displaystyle|\langle\Im G_{1}A\Im G_{2}B\rangle|\prec\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k}+\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Let us divide the matrix $B=B^{\circ}+\langle B\rangle I$ , where $B^{\circ}\in\mathbb{M}_{l}^{\circ}$ by the definition. Then, we have that

$$ \langle G_{1}AG_{2}B\rangle=\langle G_{1}AG_{2}B^{\circ}\rangle+\langle B\rangle\langle G_{2}G_{1}A\rangle\,. $$

Now, (4.14) follows from [14, (5.34)], Lemma 4.2, and equation (4.15). ∎

Then

$$ \left|\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\nu}^{\circ}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle\right|\prec\frac{\rho_{1}}{\sqrt{NL}}\left(\Lambda_{k}+\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}\right). $$

and

$$ \left|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\nu}^{\circ}}\right\rangle\right|\prec\left(\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}\right)\frac{\rho_{2}}{\sqrt{NL}}\,. $$

Using Lemma 4.1, we get

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle{A_{1}(G_{2}-m_{2}I)N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle=\left|\left\langle{G_{2}-m_{2}}\right\rangle\left\langle{A_{1}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{(G_{2}-m_{2})(N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}A_{1})^{\circ}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\prec\frac{1}{N\eta_{2}}+\frac{\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k+1}}{\sqrt{NL}}+\frac{\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k+4}}{NL}\prec\frac{\rho_{2}}{L}+\frac{\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{NL}}. $$

From Lemma 2.10, we have

$$ \left|\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}}\right\rangle\right|\prec\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{\sqrt{L}}. $$

Then from (4.12), we get

$$ \displaystyle\left(I-C\right)\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}}}\right\rangle \displaystyle=m_{1}m_{2}\left\langle{A_{1}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\bigg(\frac{1}{L}+\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{\sqrt{L}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{NL}} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{\sqrt{NL}}\left(\Lambda_{k}+\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}\right)\bigg) \displaystyle=m_{1}m_{2}\left\langle{A_{1}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\nu}}}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\bigg(\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{L}}\bigg). $$

By inverting matrix $I-C$ via a similar argument found in the proof of Lemma 3.1, we get

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}{\tilde{S}^{\circ}}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\prec 1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{L}}. $$

We now return to our bound of $\langle G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}\rangle$ . At this point, we can substitute our bounds in equation (4.22) into equation (4.11).

We have some other error terms to deal with in (4.11). By using Lemma 4.4, we have,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\prec\frac{\rho_{1}}{\sqrt{NL}}\left(\Lambda_{k}\Lambda_{k+1}+\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\prec\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}. $$

We use (4.22) and Lemma 4.1 to get

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{2}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\prec\left|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle\right|\left(\left\langle{G_{2}}\right\rangle\left|\left\langle{A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle\right|+\left|\left\langle{G_{2}\left(A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}\right)^{\circ}}\right\rangle\right|\right) \displaystyle\prec\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{L}}\right)\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+1}}{\sqrt{NL}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{NL}\right)\prec\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{L}}\right)\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{\sqrt{NL}}\right) \displaystyle\prec 1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}. $$

Using Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.1, we get

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\prec\left(\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{L\sqrt{\eta_{*}}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{L^{2}}\right)\left(\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{\sqrt{NL}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+3}}{NL}\right)\prec\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{L^{2}}\,. $$

Using Lemma 4.1, we get

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle{A_{1}(G_{2}-m_{2}I)A_{2}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq\left|\left\langle{G_{2}-m_{2}}\right\rangle\left\langle{A_{1}A_{2}}\right\rangle\right|+\left|\left\langle{(G_{2}-m_{2})(A_{2}A_{1})^{\circ}}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\prec\frac{1}{L}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+1}}{\sqrt{LN}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}}{NL}\prec\frac{1}{L}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{NL}}. $$

From Lemma 2.10, we have

$$ \left|\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}}\right\rangle\right|\prec\frac{\Lambda_{k}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}. $$

Now we use bounds (4.23), (4.24), (4.25), (4.26), (4.27) in (4.11), we have

$$ \begin{split}\left[1-\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\left(\frac{1}{N\eta_{1}}\right)\right]\left|\left\langle{G_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}\right\rangle\right|&\prec 1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}\end{split} $$

We can divide by $1-\mathcal{O}_{\prec}\left(\frac{1}{N\eta_{1}}\right)$ on both sides to derive our result. ∎

### 4.4 Bounds on $\left\langle{\Im GA\Im G^{t}A}\right\rangle$

#### Lemma 4.5.

Suppose $M$ is a diagonal traceless matrix with $\|M\|\prec 1$ . If $A_{1},A_{2}\in\mathbb{M}_{k}$ , then

$$ \left|\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}\right\rangle\right|\prec\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\left(1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+3}^{2}}{\sqrt{L}}\right)\,. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is almost identical to the proof of Lemma 3.7. We start by using the identity

$$ \begin{split}\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}\right\rangle&=\Im m_{1}\Im m_{2}\left\langle{A_{1}A_{2}}\right\rangle+\Im m_{1}\left\langle{A_{1}(\Im G_{2}^{t}-\Im m_{2}I)A_{2}}\right\rangle\\
&-m_{1}\left\langle{\underline{W\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}}\right\rangle-\Im m_{1}\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{m_{1}}{N}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{m_{1}}{N}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}\Im G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{\Im m_{1}}{N}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}G_{1}^{*}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\\
&+m_{1}\left\langle{G_{1}-m_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}\right\rangle+m_{1}\left\langle{\Im G_{1}-\Im m_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}\right\rangle\\
&+\Im m_{1}\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}-\overline{m_{1}}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{m_{1}}{N^{2}}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}G^{t}_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})A_{2}^{t}\Im G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{m_{1}}{N^{2}}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G^{t}_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})A_{2}^{t}G_{2}^{*}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{\Im m_{1}}{N^{2}}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}G^{t}_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})A_{2}^{t}\Im G_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\\
&+\frac{\Im m_{1}}{N^{2}}\sum_{\mu}\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G^{t}_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})A_{2}^{t}G_{2}^{*}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle.\end{split} $$

Like in the proof of Lemma 3.7 we use [14, (5.34),(5.35)] to get

$$ \begin{split}&\left|\left\langle{N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}\Im G_{1}}\right\rangle\left\langle{G_{1}^{*}A_{1}\Im G_{2}^{t}A_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\right|\prec\frac{\sqrt{\rho_{1}}}{N\sqrt{\eta_{1}}}\cdot\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k+1}^{2}\prec\frac{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k+1}^{2}}{\sqrt{NL}}\,,\\
&\left|\left\langle{\Im G_{1}A_{1}\Im G^{t}_{2}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})A_{2}^{t}G_{2}^{*}N\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{S}_{\mu})}\right\rangle\right|\prec\frac{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k}\Lambda_{k+1}}{\sqrt{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}}\prec\frac{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\Lambda_{k+1}^{2}}{L},\\
\end{split} $$

The second term of (4.30) is estimated differently from the diagonal case:

$$ \displaystyle|\Im m_{1}\left\langle{A_{1}(\Im G_{2}^{t}-\Im m_{2}I)A_{2}}\right\rangle| \displaystyle\leq\rho_{1}|\left\langle{\Im G_{2}^{t}-\Im m_{2}I}\right\rangle\left\langle{A_{2}A_{1}}\right\rangle|+\rho_{1}|\left\langle{\Im G_{2}^{t}(A_{2}A_{1})^{\circ}}\right\rangle| \displaystyle\prec\frac{\rho_{1}\rho_{2}}{L}+\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\left(\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{\sqrt{NL}}+\frac{\Lambda_{k+3}}{NL}\right)\,. $$

The bounds for the other terms in (4.30) can be obtained similarly. ∎

### 4.5 Proof of Main Result

We now have enough results to prove our main Theorem 2.6.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.6 .

The result of Lemma 4.3 combined with Lemma 2.7 shows that,

$$ \Lambda_{k}^{2}\prec 1+\frac{\Lambda_{k+4}^{2}}{\sqrt{J}}. $$

Starting from $k=1$ and iterating this bound shows that,

$$ \Lambda_{1}^{2}\prec 1+\frac{\Lambda_{1+4t}^{2}}{(\sqrt{J})^{t}}. $$

We can choose $t=\lceil 8/\epsilon\rceil$ and apply the trivial bound $\Lambda_{1+4t}\prec\frac{1}{\eta}$ as well as $J\geq N^{\epsilon}$ to show that $\Lambda_{1}^{2}\prec 1$ .

∎

## 5 Proof of Lemma 2.10

### 5.1 Cumulant expansion

In this section we use cumulant expansion to estimate the moments

$$ \mathbb{E}|\langle\underline{WG_{1}B_{1}G_{2}B_{2}\ldots G_{l}B_{l}}\rangle|^{2p}. $$

Parts of this section were adapted from the paper [14].

For simplicity we assume that $B_{i}\in\mathbb{M}_{k}$ for all $i\in[N]$ . It is easy to see from our proof that if $B_{i}$ are from different families $\mathbb{M}_{k}$ , each $B$ provides the corresponding $\Lambda$ in the bound.

For any $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ define a $N\times N$ matrix $\kappa^{m,n}$ , such that its entries $\kappa^{m,n}_{ab}$ are the joint cumulants of $m$ copies of $w_{ab}$ and $n$ copies of $w_{ba}$ . Note that $\kappa^{1,1}=S$ and $\kappa^{2,0}=0$ .

We use the following cumulant expansion:

$$ \mathbb{E}w_{ab}f(W)=\sum_{k=1}^{R}\sum_{m+n=k}\kappa^{m+1,n}_{ab}\mathbb{E}\partial_{ab}^{m}\partial_{ba}^{n}f(W)+\Omega_{R}, $$

where $\partial_{ab}=\partial_{w_{ab}}$ .

Applying the expansion (5.2) to (5.1) $2p$ times with respect to each $W$ allows us to express the moments (5.1) in terms of Feynman diagrams (Lemma 5.5). We understand that the following definition is quite long, but we will soon give an example that will make these concepts more concrete.

#### Definition 5.1.

Define the class of diagrams $\mathcal{G}$ as follows. Each diagram $\Gamma$ is a graph with two types of vertices $V=V_{\kappa}\cup V_{i}$ that are called $\kappa$ -vertices and internal vertices and two types of edges $E=E_{\kappa}\cup E_{g}$ called $\kappa$ -edges and $G$ -edges. For any vertex $v\in V$ its $G$ -degree $d_{g}(v)$ is defined as its degree in the graph $(V,E_{g})$ . Internal vertices $v\in V_{i}$ satisfy $d_{g}(v)=2$ and $\kappa$ -vertices can be partitioned $V_{\kappa}=\bigcup_{k\geq 2}V_{\kappa}^{k}$ according to their degree, i.e. $d_{g}(v)=k$ for $v\in V_{\kappa}^{k}$ . $\kappa$ -edges can be partitioned $e_{\kappa}=\bigcup_{k\geq 2}E_{\kappa}^{k}$ so that any $e\in E_{\kappa}^{k}$ connects two vertices from $V_{\kappa}^{k}$ .

Each $\kappa$ -edge $e=(v,w)$ carries labels $r(e)$ , $s(e)$ and the value of $\kappa^{r(e),s(e)}_{vw}$ . Each edge $e\in E_{\kappa}^{2}$ carries an additional label $h(e)\in\{\text{mat},\text{res}\}$ , which will record whether the edge comes from the derivative $\partial_{e}$ hitting a matrix $W$ or a resolvent $G_{k}$ . Each $G$ -edge $e$ has labels $i(e),t(e),*(e)\in\{0,1\}$ recording the type of the resolvent $e$ represents (imaginary part, transpose and adjoint respectively). Label $z(e)$ records the parameter of the resolvent. Labels $L(e)$ and $R(e)$ record deterministic matrices that resolvent is multiplied by.

#### Remark 5.2.

In this paper $L(e)$ and $R(e)$ will be products of matrices $B_{k}$ and $diag(\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu})$ defined in Assumption 2.1.

In addition to the definition of diagrams, we also need to introduce the notion of values associated to each diagram. On an intuitive level, a diagram represents some product of matrix quantities organized in a particular way. The following definition formalizes the exact quantity associated to each diagram.

#### Definition 5.3.

For each $\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}$ and each $e\in V_{i}$ define the value $\mathcal{G}^{e}$ of the edge $e$ as the resolvent $L(e)G(z(e))R(e)$ with imaginary part, transpose and $*$ applied according to the labels $i(e),t(e),*(e)$ . For each $e\in E_{\kappa}$ define its value $\mathcal{G}^{e}$ as $\kappa^{r(e),s(e)}$ .

Define the value of the diagram $\Gamma$ as follows.

$$ \mathrm{Val}(\Gamma)=\sum_{a_{v}\in[N],v\in V}\prod_{\{x,y\}\in E}\mathcal{G}^{\{x,y\}}_{a_{x},a_{y}} $$

Here, we construct a few examples of the diagrams that appear after applying the cumulant expansion. Let us the consider the following terms,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left|\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}B_{1}G_{2}B_{2}}}\right\rangle\right|^{2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\sum_{a,b}\kappa^{1,1}_{a,b}(G_{1}B_{1})_{bc}(G_{2}B_{2})_{ca}(B_{2}^{*}G_{2}^{*})_{ad}(B_{1}^{*}G_{1}^{*})_{db} \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}\sum_{a,b,c,d}\kappa^{1,1}_{a,b}\kappa^{1,1}_{c,d}(G_{1}B_{1}G_{2})_{bd}(G_{2}B_{2})_{ca}(B_{2}^{*}G_{2}^{*}B_{1}^{*}G_{1}^{*})_{db}(G_{1}^{*})_{ac} \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}\sum_{a,b,c,d}\kappa^{2,1}_{a,b}\kappa^{1,1}_{c,d}(G_{1})_{bd}(G_{1}B_{1}G_{2})_{ca}(G_{2}B_{2})_{ba}(B_{2}^{*}G_{2}^{*})_{db}(G_{2}^{*}B_{1}^{*}G_{1}^{*})_{ac} \displaystyle+\ldots $$

Figure 1 shows the diagram corresponding to the first term of (5.4). Each edge has its value written next to it. On the right of Figure 1 we show the edge labels in more detail. Figure 2 shows the diagrams corresponding to the other two terms of (5.4).

*Figure 1: Diagram on the left corresponds to the first term of (5.4). On the right we show all labels of the edge $\{d,b\}$ with value $B_{1}^{*}G_{1}^{*}$ .*

*Figure 2: The diagrams corresponding to the second and third terms of (5.4).*

The following definition is similar to the properties (P1)-(P8) in Proposition 5.3 of [14]. The main purpose of the definition is to encompass the properties of the graphs produced by cumulant expansion that are most important for our later counting bound. We remark that most of these properties are mechanical consequences of considering the algorithm of cumulant expansion.

#### Definition 5.4.

A diagram is said to be $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ -regular if there exist a subset $V_{o}$ of orthogonality vertices such that the following condition holds:

- 1. The graph $(V_{\kappa},E_{\kappa})$ is a perfect matching.

- 2. The internal vertices satisfies $|V_{i}|=2(l-1)p$ . The edges satisfy $1\leq|E_{\kappa}|\leq 2p$ , $\#\{e\in E_{g}:i(e)=1\}=2ip$ , and $|E_{g}|=\sum_{e\in E_{\kappa}}d_{g}(e)+2(l-1)p\geq 2p$ .

- 3. For any $\kappa$ edge $(uv)\in E_{\kappa}^{k}$ , the $G$ -degrees of $u,v\in V_{\kappa}$ satisfy $d^{in}_{g}(u)=d^{out}_{g}(v)$ , $d^{in}_{g}(v)=d^{out}_{g}(u)$ , and $d_{g}(u)=d_{g}(v)\geq 2$ . We can define the $G$ -degree of $(uv)$ as $d_{g}(uv):=d_{g}(u)=d_{g}(v)=k$ .

- 4. Every $E_{g}$ -cycle on $V_{\kappa}^{2}\cup V_{i}$ contains at least two vertices in $V_{\kappa}^{2}$ .

- 5. Denoting the number of isolated cycles in $(V_{\kappa}\cup V_{i},E_{g})$ with at most $k$ vertices in $V_{o}$ by $n_{cyc}^{o=k}$ , we have $2n_{cyc}^{o=0}+n_{cyc}^{o=1}\leq 2|E_{\kappa}^{2}|-|V_{o}\cap V_{\kappa}^{2}|$ .

- 6. $|V_{i}\cap V_{o}|=2p(a+t-\mathbf{1}\{l\in\mathfrak{a}\cup\mathfrak{t}\})$ .

- 7. If $l\in\mathfrak{a}\cup\mathfrak{t}$ , then $2|E^{2}_{\kappa}|+|E^{\geq 3}_{\kappa}|-2p\leq|V_{o}\cap V_{\kappa}^{2}|\leq 2p$ , otherwise $V_{o}\cap V_{\kappa}^{2}$ is empty.

- 8. For any $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge $e$ , the number of its endpoint in $V_{o}$ is either $0$ if $h(e)=\text{mat}$ , or at most $1$ if $h(e)=\text{res}$ .

With the notion of diagrams in hand, we can now describe the the graph produced by cumulant expansion, which reduces the computations of moments of our renormalization terms to quantities defined on our $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ regular graphs.

#### Lemma 5.5 (Cumulant expansion).

For any $p\in\mathbb{N}$ , there is a collection of graphs $\mathcal{G}^{av}_{p}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}|\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}B_{1}...G_{l}B_{l}}}\right\rangle|^{2p}=\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}^{av}_{p}}\mathbb{E}\mathrm{Val}(\Gamma)+O(N^{-2p})\,. $$

Furthermore, for all diagrams in $\mathcal{G}^{av}_{p}$ are “ $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ -regular” in the sense of Definition 5.4.

#### Proof.

This is the result of Proposition 5.3 in [14]. The only modification we make is the additional property 8 from Definition 5.4. This property holds because the vertices from $V_{\kappa}^{2}$ can only be selected as orthogonality vertices if they appear as a result of the derivative acting on a $G$ (see (orth-2) in the proof of Proposition 5.3 in [14]). ∎

In our proof we need to emphasize another property of the diagrams appearing in equation (5.5).

#### Lemma 5.6.

For any $\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}_{p}^{av}$ and any $\kappa^{1,1}$ -edge $e$ with $h(e)=\text{res}$ , one of its endpoint has one outgoing $G$ -edge $e^{\prime}$ with $L(e^{\prime})=I$ and one incoming edge $e^{\prime\prime}$ with $R(e^{\prime\prime})=I$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose $e=(ab)$ comes from the cumulant expansion with respect to $w_{ab}$ in $w_{ab}\langle\Delta^{ab}G_{1}B_{1}\ldots G_{l}B_{l}\rangle$ . Since $h(e)=\text{res}$ , $\partial_{ba}$ hits a resolvent $G_{k}$ , which becomes $G_{k}\Delta^{ba}G_{k}$ . Then vertex $b$ has an outgoing edge $e^{\prime}$ with resolvent $G_{1}$ and $L(e^{\prime})=I$ and an incoming edge with resolvent $G_{k}$ and $R(e)=I$ . ∎

Our final lemma computes the values of regular graphs along with the extra condition that $\kappa_{1,1}=\frac{1}{N}$ . This lemma is from [14]. The reason we cannot apply this directly to our cumulant expansion is that the value of $\kappa^{1,1}$ we use is not uniform; our work in the next section is to modify the graphs so that we can reduce the computation of our graph values to those that appear in the following lemma.

#### Lemma 5.7.

If $\Gamma_{\kappa,G}$ is $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ -regular, $\kappa^{1,1}_{xy}=\frac{1}{N}$ , $|\kappa^{p,q}_{xy}|\leq CN^{-(p+q)/2}$ , and $L(e),R(e)\in\mathbb{M}_{k}\cup\mathbb{M}_{k}^{\circ}$ for all $G$ -edges $e$ , then

$$ \mathrm{Val}(\Gamma_{\kappa,G})\prec\begin{cases}\rho^{2(b+1)p}N^{2bp}L^{-2bp},&b=l\,,\\
\Lambda_{k}^{2(a+t)p}\rho^{2ip\vee 2(b+1)p}N^{p(a+t+2b)}L^{-p(1+2b)},&b<l\,,\end{cases} $$

where $b:=l-a-t$ .

### 5.2 The Graph Splitting Procedure

We remark that there is only one difference between the case that we are considering here and the diagrams from [14]: they use the fact that the lowest order cumulants $\kappa^{1,1}$ are all uniformly $\frac{1}{N}$ . This allows them to re-express some of the quantities related to the diagrams in terms of traces of matrix products. This is the key step that allows them to apply Proposition 5.6 to bound the value of the graph. In the absence of this important condition, what we must do is find a way to take our graphs into an expression that would be useful.

We find a procedure that takes any diagram $\Gamma$ and re-expresses it as a sum of other diagrams. Namely,

$$ \text{Val}(\Gamma)=\sum_{\mu}\mathrm{Val}(\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu}). $$

The details of our transformation will show that the diagrams $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu}$ are $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ -regular diagrams along with the property that the new ‘ $\kappa^{1,1}$ ’ edges have value $\frac{1}{N}$ . Formally, we find another way to write the covariance matrices $\kappa^{1,1}$ and incorporate these terms into one of the $L$ or $R$ matrices that multiply the $G$ . The end result of this procedure is to formally treat the old $\kappa^{1,1}$ edges as having value $\frac{1}{N}$ . We now begin to describe this procedure more formally.

For every $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge, we will decompose the diagram $\Gamma$ into $N+1$ further diagrams. Thus, if we let $E_{2}$ be the set of all $\kappa^{1,1}$ edges, we will decompose $\Gamma$ into $(N+1)^{|E_{2}|}$ edges. The graph splitting procedure essentially treats every edge independently, so to describe the construction, it is best to consider the case that there is only a single $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge.

First, consider a $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge $e=(x,y)$ . In case $h(e)=res$ , we know from Lemma 5.6 that one of $x$ or $y$ has the property that it has a single incoming edge with $R(e)=I$ and a single outgoing edge with $L(e)=I$ . Assume that this vertex is $x$ . When we split $\kappa^{1,1}$ later, then this property allow us to introduce a trace 0 matrix in a location that is useful for cancellations. We remark that by Definition 5.4 (1) if there were more $\kappa^{1,1}$ edges, this vertex $x$ would not be shared with the other $\kappa^{1,1}$ edges. In case $h(e)=mat$ , $x$ can be chosen arbitrarily among the two vertices adjacent to the $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge.

We have the following matrix decomposition of $S_{xy}:=\kappa^{1,1}_{x,y}$ .

$$ S_{xy}=\sum_{\mu}\tilde{S}_{x\mu}\tilde{S}_{\mu y}. $$

Though this procedure formally introduces the vertex $\mu$ , these vertices will not be introduced into our diagram. Instead, the first $N$ of $N+1$ diagrams will be indexed by this vertex $\mu$ ; we call these diagrams $\tilde{\Gamma}^{1},\ldots,\tilde{\Gamma}^{N}$ . The remaining graph we will call $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ , and will be derived via a more complicated resummation procedure.

After fixing a value of $\mu$ , we still have to perform more manipulation in order to derive the diagrams $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu}$ . This procedure is quite similar to those performed in Sections 3 and 4; namely, we further split $\tilde{S}_{x\mu}$ and interpret this as a trace $0$ matrix. Recall the traceless part as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{x\mu}=\tilde{S}_{x\mu}-\frac{1}{N} \displaystyle\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}=\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}-\left\langle{\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}}\right\rangle=\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}-\frac{1}{N}. $$

We define the diagram $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu}$ as follows. We take the diagram $\Gamma$ and redefine labels so that for the incoming edge to vertex $x$ , we multiply $R$ on the right by $N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}^{\circ}_{\mu}$ . At $y$ , we change the label so that at the incoming edge to $y$ , we multiply $R$ on the right by $N\mathrm{diag}\tilde{S}_{\mu}$ . Finally, we change the value of $\kappa^{1,1}$ formally to $\frac{1}{N}$ on the edge $\{x,y\}$ .

In case $h(e)=res$ , the main benefit is that even though we remove the orthogonality at vertex $y$ , vertex $x$ becomes a trace zero orthogonality vertex. Thus, there is no net loss in the number of orthogonality vertices in all of the diagrams $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu}$ for $\mu$ between $1$ and $N$ . Moreover, the traceless matrix involved in this new orthogonality vertex is in $\mathbb{M}_{0}^{\circ}$ .

In case $h(e)=mat$ , neither $x$ nor $y$ are orthogonality vertices of $\Gamma$ , so our procedure doesn’t affect $V_{o}$ .

Finally, we define our final diagram $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ by taking the diagram $\Gamma$ and changing the label $\kappa^{1,1}$ to $\frac{1}{N}$ at the edge $\{x,y\}$ . It is easy to check that

$$ \mathrm{Val}(\Gamma)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu=1}^{N}\mathrm{Val}(\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu})+\mathrm{Val}(\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{ext}})\,. $$

Here is an example of the graph splitting procedure. We only draw the verteces and edges that connect to the $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge.

#### Lemma 5.8.

The diagrams $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mu}$ or $\tilde{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ that have been constructed are $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ -regular diagrams.

#### Proof.

Let $e=(x,y)$ be the single $\kappa^{1,1}$ edge in the original diagram $\Gamma$ .

The only modifications that we have to the diagrams $\tilde{\Gamma}^{i}$ from the original diagram $\Gamma$ are in the labels of the edges are are adjacent to the vertices $(x,y)$ . In addition, vertices $x$ and $y$ are our only possible changes for $V_{o}$ . From this property, it is clear to see that properties 1-4 of Definition 5.4 still hold after the modification. Furthermore, property 5 of Definition 5.4 is a consequence of property 4 regardless of the choice of $V_{o}$ . This is a simple counting argument.

With regards to the sets of vertices $V_{o}$ , we describe a bit more elaborately what changes are made. Due to property $8$ of Definition 5.4, we know that at most one of $x$ and $y$ is in the set $V_{o}$ . Recall that we have earlier chosen the vertex $x$ to lie between the product of two pure $G$ matrices without any intermittent matrix product. Once we multiply in between the two pure $G$ matrices at $x$ by the matrix $\text{diag}(\tilde{S}^{\circ})_{\mu}$ , we see that $x$ is in $V^{0tr}$ of $\tilde{\Gamma}^{i}$ . Regardless of whether $x\in V_{o}$ or $y\in V_{o}$ in the graph $\Gamma$ , we put the vertex $x$ into $V_{o}$ for $\tilde{\Gamma}^{i}$ . Thus, the cardinality of any the sets $V_{o}$ and $V_{o}\cap V_{\kappa}^{2}$ do not change. Thus, properties 6-8 of Definition 5.4 still hold. ∎

The previous discussion has established the following lemma.

#### Lemma 5.9.

Every $\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}_{p}$ can be split into a set of diagrams, $\widetilde{\Gamma}^{(\mu_{1},...,\mu_{m})}$ for $\mu_{i}\in[n]\cup\{0\},1\leq i\leq m$ with $m$ being the number of $\kappa^{1,1}$ edges in $\Gamma$ , in the sense that

$$ \mathrm{Val}(\Gamma_{\kappa,G})=\sum_{\mu_{i}\in[n]\cup\{\mathrm{ext}\},1\leq i\leq m}\Big(\frac{1}{N}\Big)^{\#\{i:\mu_{i}\not=\mathrm{ext}\}}\mathrm{Val}(\widetilde{\Gamma}^{(\mu_{1},...,\mu_{m})}_{\kappa^{\prime},G})\,, $$

where ${\kappa^{\prime}}^{1,1}=\frac{1}{N}$ and ${\kappa^{\prime}}^{p,q}={\kappa}^{p,q}$ for $(p,q)\not=(1,1)$ . Furthermore, all of the diagrams $\widetilde{\Gamma}^{(\mu_{1},...,\mu_{m})}_{\kappa^{\prime},G}$ are $(l,p,i,\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{t})$ -regular.

#### Proof of Lemma 2.10.

The high probability estimates on $\left\langle{\underline{WG_{1}A_{1}G_{2}A_{2}}}\right\rangle$ and other similar quantities are readily derived by computing high moments and applying Markov’s inequality. The cumulant expansion Lemma 5.5 gives an expression of the moments in terms of values of graphs. The values of these graphs are determined by the splitting procedure in Lemma 5.9 and the evaluation of graph values in appropriate conditions as in Lemma 5.7. The combinatorics of the sum over graphs is exactly the same as that of [14] and we can derive the exact same estimates. ∎

# Solution of Matrix Dyson Equation for Random Matrices with Fast Correlation Decay

**Authors:** Sofiia Dubova V.N. Karazin Kharkiv National University

## Abstract

We consider the solution of Matrix Dyson Equation $-M\left(z\right)^{-1}=z+\mathcal{S}\left(M\left(z\right)\right)$ , where entries of the linear operator $\mathcal{S}:\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ decay exponentially. We show that $M(z)$ also has exponential off-diagonal decay and can be represented as Laurent series with coefficients determined by entries of $\mathcal{S}$ . We also prove that for Hermitian random matrices with exponential correlation decay empirical density converges to the deterministic density obtained from $M(z)$ . These results have already been proved in [1] with the resolvent method, here we give an alternate proof via conceptually much simpler moment method.

AMS Subject Classification (2010): 60B20.

Keywords: Correlated random matrices, Matrix Dyson equation.

## 1 Introduction

For Wigner matrices, i.e. Hermitian random matrices with centered i.i.d. entries, it has long been known that the empirical density of eigenvalues converges to the deterministic density $\rho$ called self-consistent density of states. Here $\rho$ is the semicircle density.

By dropping the assumption of identical distribution of entries, one gets a more general class of matrices, called the Wigner-type ensemble. For Wigner-type random matrix $H=(h_{xy})_{x,y=1}^{N}$ self-consistent density of states can be determined from the solution of vector equation

$$ -m_{x}(z)^{-1}=z+[Sm(z)]_{x}, $$

where $S=(S_{xy})_{x,y=1}^{N}$ is the matrix of variances, i.e. $S_{xy}=\mathbb{E}|h_{xy}|^{2}$ . The solution $m(z)=(m_{1}(z),\ldots,m_{N}(z))$ is a vector-valued function defined on the upper half plane $\mathbb{H}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Im}\,z>0\}$ and it satisfies the additional condition $\mathrm{Im}\,m_{x}(z)>0$ . The solution is unique analytic function on $\mathbb{H}$ . The average of the entries of vector $m(z)$ is the Stieltjes transform of the self-consistent density of states $\rho$ , i.e.

$$ \langle m(z)\rangle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x=1}^{N}m_{x}(z)=\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\rho(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau}{\tau-z}. $$

The solution $m(z)$ has been studied in [4] and [6]. It was shown that $m(z)$ can be expressed as Laurent series for large $|z|$ . The coefficients are expressed explicitly through the entries of variance matrix $S$ .

In this paper we consider a more general class of random matrices. We replace the condition of independence of the entries by the condition on fast correlation decay. This means that the correlation of the entries decreases exponentially with the increase in distance between the entries in the matrix. For such random matrix $H$ of the size $N\times N$ consider the operator $\mathcal{S}:\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ defined by covariances of the entries. More precisely, $\mathcal{S}(R)=\mathbb{E}HRH$ for each $R\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ . The self-consistent density of states can be obtained from the solution of Matrix Dyson Equation (MDE):

$$ -M\left(z\right)^{-1}=z+\mathcal{S}\left(M\left(z\right)\right), $$

where $M(z)$ is a matrix-valued function defined on $\mathbb{H}$ . Additionally, we are only interested in the solution of MDE with positive imaginary part, i.e. ${\mathrm{Im}\,M(z)>0}$ . Positivity is meant in the sense of scalar product $\langle R,T\rangle:=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,R^{*}T$ in the space of matrices $\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ .

MDE was studied in [5]. It has unique solution $M(z)$ holomorphic on $\mathbb{H}$ . In the first part of the paper we generalize the results from [4] and [6] on the Laurent series representation of the solution of (1.1). We express solution of MDE as the Laurent series with coefficients expressed in terms of the entries of operator $\mathcal{S}$ . Using this formula, we prove off-diagonal decay of the solution for large $|z|$ (see Theorem 2.1).

In the other part of the paper we prove that the empirical distribution of eigenvalues converges to the self-consistent density of states obtained as the inverse Stieltjes transform of $\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,M(z)$ using moment method.

Both results in this paper have already been achieved in [1] with the resolvent method and by fairly involved analysis of the matrix Dyson equation. The main goal here is to give shorter and conceptually simpler alternative proofs and demonstrate that the moment method extends to correlated Wigner matrices.

Acknowledgment: This work was done during a summer internship at László Erdős’ research group at IST Austria. The author is very grateful to him for suggesting the problem and for permanent help and guidance during the entire project.

## 2 Main results

### 2.1 Frame of the tree

First, we introduce some notation needed for formulation of our result.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{k}$ denote the set of the rooted ordered trees $\Gamma=\left(V(\Gamma),E(\Gamma)\right)$ with $k$ edges. The ordering means the following additional structure on the rooted tree: for every vertex $v\in V(\Gamma)$ the set of children of $v$ is ordered, i.e. children of $v$ are $w_{1}<w_{2}<\ldots<w_{c(v)}$ , where $c(v)$ is the number of children of $v$ . For every child $w$ of the vertex $v$ one could define the position of $w$ in the sequence of children of $v$ . Let $n(w)$ denote this position. Since any vertex $w\in V(\Gamma)\setminus\{root\}$ has exactly one parent, $n(w)$ is defined for any such vertex. It is easy to see that the ordering uniquely defines an oriented realization of the tree in the plane, two planar trees being equivalent if they can be deformed into each other by an orientation preserving homeomorphism of the plane.

Every edge $e\in E(\Gamma)$ is incident with two vertices denoted by $e_{-},e_{+}\in V(\Gamma)$ , where the sign indicates child-parent relation, i.e. $e_{+}$ is a child of $e_{-}$ .

For every ordered tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ one could walk around $\Gamma$ starting in the root and each step going from vertex $v$ to the first not yet visited child of $v$ or to the parent of $v$ if all children of $v$ have already been visited. Note that the walk ends at the root of $\Gamma$ and consists of $2k$ steps. This allows us to define the frame of $\Gamma$ denoted by $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ , which is the path graph with $2k$ edges, fixed direction and association of its vertices with the vertices of $\Gamma$ defined by the following procedure. We start at the first vertex of the path and associate it with the root of $\Gamma$ . Then, as we walk around $\Gamma$ , each step the next vertex in the path is associated with the vertex of $\Gamma$ where this step arrives. This procedure also gives the association of each edge of the frame with the edge of $\Gamma$ , as each step of the walk corresponds to the edge of $\Gamma$ .

For $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{0}$ the frame $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ is a graph with one vertex and no edges.

Given the oriented planar realization of $\Gamma$ , one could draw the frame of $\Gamma$ as the path starting at the vertex near the root of $\Gamma$ and going around the tree in counter-clockwise direction with each vertex drawn near its associated vertex and each edge running parallel with the associated edge of $\Gamma$ (see Figure 1).

*Figure 1: Tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{5}$ and its frame $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma).$*

Denote $\left[N\right]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ . It is easy to see that for each vertex $v\in V(\Gamma)$ there are $c(v)+1$ vertices of $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ associated with $v$ . For every $v\in V(\Gamma)$ we denote the vertices of $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ associated with $v$ by $p_{0}^{v},p_{1}^{v},\ldots,p_{c(v)}^{v}$ in the order of appearance in the frame. We now label the vertices of $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ by assigning a number from $\left[N\right]$ to each of them. More precisely, the vertex $p_{n}^{v}\in\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ is labelled with a number $x_{n}^{v}\in\left[N\right]$ . A labelling of $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ is a set of arrays $\mathbf{x}=\{\mathbf{x}(v)=(x_{0}^{v},x_{1}^{v},\ldots,x_{c(v)}^{v})\mid v\in V(\Gamma)\}$ . Let $\mathcal{X}(\Gamma)$ denote the set of the labellings of $\mathcal{F}(\Gamma)$ . Sets of the labellings with fixed first and last labels are denoted by

$$ \mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma):=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}(\Gamma)\mid x_{0}^{root}=a,\ x_{c(root)}^{root}=b\},\>a,b\in[N]. $$

### 2.2 Solution of MDE

In this section we present our result on the form of MDE solution and its off-diagonal decay in large $|z|$ regime. The proofs are presented in the section 3.

MDE has been studied in [5]. It has unique solution $M(z)$ with positive imaginary part for $z\in\mathbb{H}=\{\zeta\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta>0\}$ . Moreover, the solution holomorphic on $\mathbb{H}$ .

First, we formalize the idea of off-diagonal decay. Define the scalars $\mathcal{S}_{ab,cd}$ for the operator $\mathcal{S}$ by the identity

$$ \left[\mathcal{S}(R)\right]_{xt}=\sum_{y,z=1}^{N}\mathcal{S}_{xy,zt}R_{yz} $$

for any $R\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ .

We introduce norms on the space of matrices and on operators acting on matrices that reflect exponential decay of the matrix elements as they go farther from the diagonal.

For every matrix $R=(R_{xy})_{x,y=1}^{N}$ and $l>0$ we introduce the $l$ -norm of $R$ :

$$ \|R\|_{l}=\max_{x,y=1}^{N}e^{\frac{1}{l}|x-y|}|R_{xy}|. $$

Similarly we define the $l$ -norm of the operator $\mathcal{S}:\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ :

$$ \|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}=\max_{x,y,z,t=1}^{N}e^{\frac{1}{l}\rho(xy,zt)}|\mathcal{S}_{xy,zt}|, $$

where

$$ \rho(xy,zt):=\min\{|x-z|+|y-t|,|x-t|+|y-z|\} $$

is the symmetrized distance between the index pairs $(xy)$ and $(zt)$ .

For every tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ define the matrix $\mathrm{val}(\Gamma)=\left(\mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)\right)_{a,b=1}^{N}$ , where

$$ \mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma):=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\mathcal{S}_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}},x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}. $$

Note that the edges of the frame connecting the vertices with labels $x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}$ , $x_{0}^{e_{+}}$ and the vertices with labels $x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}$ , $x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}$ are associated with the edge $e$ of $\Gamma$ .

For $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{0}$ we define $\mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma):=\delta_{a=b}$ .

#### Theorem 2.1.

Suppose for some $l>0$ and some constant $c>0$ operator $\mathcal{S}$ has finite $l$ -norm and $\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}\leq\frac{c}{N}$ . Then for any $\varepsilon>0$ there is a constant $R(l,\varepsilon)$ such that the solution of the Matrix Dyson Equation for $|z|^{2}>R(l,\varepsilon)$ is given by Laurent series

$$ M(z)=-\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C_{k}z^{-2k-1}, $$

where

$$ C_{k}:=\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}}\mathrm{val}(\Gamma) $$

for any nonnegative integer $k$ .

Moreover, the solution $M(z)$ has finite $(1+\varepsilon)l$ -norm for $|z|^{2}>R(l,\varepsilon)$ .

### 2.3 Random matrices with exponentially decaying correlations

For any positive integer $N$ consider $N\times N$ Hermitian random matrix $H=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}W$ , where $W=(w_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{N}$ . Let $W$ satisfy the following assumptions:

- (A) (Finite moments) For all positive integers $k$ there exists a constant $\mu_{k}$ such that

$$ \mathbb{E}|w_{xy}|^{k}\leq\mu_{k} $$

(2.7) for any $x,y\in[N]$ .

- (B) (Decay of the cumulants) The cumulants of the entries of $w$ decay exponentially. More precisely, for some $l>0$ , constant $c$ and any $x,y,z,t\in[N]$

$$ |\kappa(w_{xy},w_{zt})|\leq ce^{-\frac{1}{l}\rho(xy,zt)} $$

(2.8) and for any $k\geq 3$ and any $x_{1},y_{1},\ldots,x_{k},y_{k}\in[N]$ the following inequality holds:

$$ |\kappa(w_{x_{1}y_{1}},\ldots,w_{x_{k}y_{k}})|\leq\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T_{min})}|\kappa(w_{x_{i}y_{i}},w_{x_{j}y_{j}})|, $$

(2.9) where $T_{min}$ is the minimal spanning tree of the complete graph with vertices $1,\ldots,k$ and edge length $d(\{i,j\})=\rho(x_{i}y_{i},x_{j}y_{j})$ (see (2.4) for the definition of $\rho$ ).

These assumptions are the exponential analogue of assumptions made in [3].

Consider the Matrix Dyson Equation with operator $\mathcal{S}$ such that ${\mathcal{S}(R)=\mathbb{E}HRH}$ for any $R\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ . Then $\mathcal{S}_{xy,zt}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}w_{xy}w_{zt}$ .

Let $\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{N}$ be eigenvalues of $H$ . Define the empirical distribution of the eigenvalues:

$$ L^{(N)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{\lambda_{j}}. $$

Consider the Stieltjes transform of $L^{N}$ :

$$ S^{(N)}(z)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)}{x-z} $$

defined on upper half of the complex plane $\mathbb{H}$ .

#### Theorem 2.2.

Under the assumptions (A) and (B), the conditions of the Theorem 2.1 hold and $\mathbb{E}S^{(N)}(z)-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,M(z)$ converges to 0 for all $z\in\mathbb{H}$ .

In the Section 4 we get this result by proving convergence of the moments of empirical distribution to the normalized trace of $C_{k}$ from (2.6).

Theorem 2.2 implies that the averaged empirical measure $\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}$ converges weakly to the self-consistent density of states $\rho$ obtained as inverse Stieltjes transform of $\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,M(z)$ . One could prove that empirical density $L^{(N)}$ converges weakly in probability to $\rho$ using similar technique.

## 3 Solution of MDE

### 3.1 Decomposition of the ordered tree

For any two trees $\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{1}}$ and $\Gamma_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{2}}$ define a new tree $\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\oplus\Gamma_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{1}+n_{2}+1}$ with

$$ \displaystyle V(\Gamma)=V(\Gamma_{1})\cup V(\Gamma_{2}), \displaystyle E(\Gamma)=E(\Gamma_{1})\cup E(\Gamma_{2})\cup\{\{root(\Gamma_{1}),root(\Gamma_{2})\}\}. $$

The root of $\Gamma_{1}$ is the root of $\Gamma$ and $root(\Gamma_{2})$ is the last child of $root(\Gamma)$ . Ordering of the children of every other vertex is the same as the ordering of children of the corresponding vertices of $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ (for example, see Figure …). Every tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ can be uniquely decomposed as $\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\oplus\Gamma_{2}$ , where $\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{1}}$ , $\Gamma_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{2}}$ and $n_{1}+n_{2}=k-1$ (for details see [4]). Note that the operation $\oplus$ is not commutative.

The frame of $\Gamma$ can be naturally split into the frames of $\Gamma_{1}$ , $\Gamma_{2}$ and two edges associated with the edge $\{root(\Gamma_{1}),root(\Gamma_{2})\}$ of $\Gamma$ .

### 3.2 Explicit form of the solution of MDE

#### Lemma 3.1.

For every $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$

$$ \mathrm{val}(\Gamma)=\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{1})\mathcal{S}(\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{2})), $$

where $\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\oplus\Gamma_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $v$ denote the last child of the root of $\Gamma$ , i.e. the root of $\Gamma_{2}$ . For a labelling $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)$ and fixed $c,d,e\in[N]$ , consider the labellings $\mathbf{x}$ with $x_{c(root)-1}^{root}=c$ , $x_{0}^{v}=d$ and $x_{c(v)}^{v}=e$ . Then $\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2})$ is naturally split into two labellings $\mathbf{x}_{1}\in\mathcal{X}_{ac}(\Gamma_{1})$ and $\mathbf{x}_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{de}(\Gamma_{2})$ . Therefore, (3.1) is equivalent to

$$ \mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)=\sum_{c,d,e=1}^{N}\mathrm{val}_{ac}(\Gamma_{1})\mathcal{S}_{cd,eb}\ \mathrm{val}_{de}(\Gamma_{2}). $$

By definition of the scalars $\mathcal{S}_{cd,eb}$ ,

$$ \sum_{d,e=1}^{N}\mathcal{S}_{cd,eb}\ \mathrm{val}_{de}(\Gamma_{2})=\left[\mathcal{S}(\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{2}))\right]_{cb}. $$

Plugging in (3.3) into (3.2) we obtain

$$ \mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)=\sum_{c=1}^{N}\mathrm{val}_{ac}(\Gamma_{1})\left[\mathcal{S}(\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{2}))\right]_{cb}=\left[\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{1})\mathcal{S}(\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{2}))\right]_{ab}. $$

∎

Now we introduce the solution of MDE in the large $|z|$ regime.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Suppose that for some matrix norm $\|C_{k}\|\leq CR^{k}$ for any $k$ with some constants $C$ and $R$ (see (2.6) for the definition of $C_{k}$ ). Then the Laurent series (2.5) gives the solution of the Matrix Dyson Equation (1.2), defined on the domain of absolute convergence of the series (2.5), in particular for any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|z|^{2}>R$ .

#### Proof.

Notice that for $z\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|z|^{2}>R$ the series (2.5) absolutely converges in the sense of the norm $\|.\|$ .

Multiplying MDE by $M(z)$ and introducing $U(z):=-zM(z)$ we obtain

$$ U(z)=I+z^{-2}U(z)\mathcal{S}(U(z)), $$

where $I$ is identity matrix.

Plugging in the form of the solution $U(z)=\sum_{0}^{\infty}C_{k}z^{-2k}$ into (3.4) and equating the coefficients, we get

$$ C_{k}=\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}C_{k-1-m}\mathcal{S}(C_{m}). $$

Since for every $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ there is unique $m\in\{0,1,\ldots k-1\}$ and unique trees $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ such that $\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\oplus\Gamma_{2}$ , identity (3.5) is equivalent to

$$ \sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}}\mathrm{val}(\Gamma)=\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}}\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{1})\mathcal{S}(\mathrm{val}(\Gamma_{2})), $$

which follows from Lemma 3.1.

∎

### 3.3 Convergence and exponential decay of the solution of MDE

#### Lemma 3.3.

For every positive integer $k$ and for any $\varepsilon>0$ and $x\geq 0$

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}e^{-\left(|x-y_{1}|+|y_{1}-y_{2}|+\ldots+|y_{k}|\right)}dy_{1}\ldots dy_{k}\leq\left(2\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k-1}e^{-\frac{x}{1+\varepsilon}}. $$

#### Proof.

We introduce the function $f(x)=e^{-|x|}$ . Notice that the LHS of (3.6) is the $k$ -fold convolution of $f(x)$ , denoted by $f^{*k}(x)$ . Fourier transform of $f$ is

$$ \mathcal{F}f(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-ixt}f(x)dx=\frac{2}{t^{2}+1}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \left(\mathcal{F}f^{*k}\right)(t)=\left(\mathcal{F}f(t)\right)^{k}=\left(\frac{2}{t^{2}+1}\right)^{k}. $$

Since $f^{*k}(x)$ and its Fourier transform are absolutely integrable, we have

$$ f^{*k}(x)=\mathcal{F}^{-1}\left(\mathcal{F}f^{*k}\right)(t)=\frac{2^{k}}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{ixt}}{(t^{2}+1)^{k}}dt. $$

Consider the function $g(z)=\frac{e^{ixz}}{(z^{2}+1)^{k}}$ on the complex plane and a contour $C_{R}$ with positive orientation, which is the concatenation of the semicircle $C_{R}^{1}=\{Re^{i\theta}\mid\theta\in[0,\pi]\}$ and the segment $C_{R}^{2}=[-R,R]$ with some large $R$ . Integrating $g(z)$ over $C_{R}$ we get

$$ \oint_{C_{R}}g(z)dz=\int_{C_{R}^{1}}g(z)dz+\int_{-R}^{R}\frac{e^{ixt}}{(t^{2}+1)^{k}}dt. $$

Notice that $\left|\frac{1}{(z^{2}+1)^{k}}\right|\leq\frac{1}{(R^{2}-1)^{k}}$ on the semicircle $C_{R}$ with $R>1$ . Hence, for $x>0$ the integral $\int_{C_{R}^{1}}g(z)dz$ vanishes as $R$ goes to infinity by Jordan’s lemma. Similarly, for $x=0$ :

$$ \left|\int_{C_{R}^{1}}\frac{1}{(z^{2}+1)^{k}}dz\right|\leq length(C_{R}^{1})\cdot\frac{1}{(R^{2}-1)^{k}}=\frac{\pi R}{(R^{2}-1)^{k}}\rightarrow 0. $$

For $R>1$ , the function $g(z)$ has a pole of order $k$ at $z=i$ inside the contour $C_{R}$ . Hence, by residue theorem,

$$ \oint_{C_{R}}g(z)dz=2\pi i\cdot res_{i}g(z)=\frac{2\pi i}{(k-1)!}\lim_{z\rightarrow i}\frac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}\left[(z-i)^{k}g(z)\right]. $$

Plugging in (3.9) into (3.8) and letting $R$ go to infinity we get

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{ixt}}{(t^{2}+1)^{k}}dt=\frac{2\pi i}{(k-1)!}\lim_{z\rightarrow i}\frac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}\left[e^{ixz}(z+i)^{-k}\right]=\\
=\frac{2\pi i}{(k-1)!}\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{m}(ix)^{k-1-m}e^{-x}(-k)\ldots(-k-(m-1))(2i)^{-k-m}. $$

Combining (3.10) with (3.7) and taking absolute value of $f^{*k}$ we obtain

$$ \left|f^{*k}(x)\right|\leq\frac{2^{k}}{(k-1)!}e^{-x}\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{m}x^{k-1-m}\frac{(k+m-1)!}{(k-1)!}2^{-k-m}. $$

Notice that

$$ \frac{1}{(k-1)!}\binom{k-1}{m}\frac{(k+m-1)!}{(k-1)!}=\binom{k+m-1}{k-1}\frac{1}{(k-1-m)!} $$

Estimating the binomial coefficient with $\binom{k+m-1}{k-1}\leq 2^{k+m-1}$ and multiplying powers of $2$ , we get

$$ \left|f^{*k}(x)\right|\leq 2^{k-1}e^{-x}\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\frac{1}{(k-1-m)!}x^{k-1-m}. $$

Using the inequality $x^{k-1-m}\leq\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}x\right)^{k-1-m}\cdot\left(\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k-1}$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ , we see that

$$ \left|f^{*k}(x)\right|\leq\left(2\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k-1}e^{-x}\sum_{m=0}^{k-1}\frac{1}{(k-1-m)!}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}x\right)^{k-1-m}\\
\leq\left(2\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k-1}e^{-x}e^{\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}x}=\left(2\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k-1}e^{-\frac{x}{1+\varepsilon}}. $$

∎

#### Lemma 3.4.

For fixed $l>0$ and for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a constant $c(l,\varepsilon)>1$ such that for any nonnegative integer $k$ and any $a,b\in[N]$ the following inequality holds:

$$ Path^{(l)}_{k+1}(a,b):=\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}=1}^{N}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|a-x_{1}|+|x_{1}-x_{2}|+\ldots+|x_{k}-b|\right)}\\
\leq c(l,\varepsilon)^{k+1}e^{-\frac{1}{(1+\varepsilon)l}|a-b|}. $$

#### Remark 1.

We define $Path^{(l)}_{0}(a,b)=\delta_{a=b}$ . Note that (3.12) holds for $k=-1$ .

#### Proof.

For $k=0$ inequality (3.12) holds. Assume $k\geq 1$ . Without loss of generality assume that $a\geq b$ . Adding new summands and the summation indices from $x_{i}$ to $x_{i}-b$ , we obtain

$$ Path^{(l)}_{k+1}(a,b)\leq\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}=-N}^{N}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|(a-b)-x_{1}|+|x_{1}-x_{2}|+\ldots+|x_{k}|\right)}. $$

We claim that for fixed $x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}$

$$ e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|(a-b)-x_{1}|+|x_{1}-x_{2}|+\ldots+|x_{k}|\right)}\leq\\
\leq e^{\frac{1}{l}k}\int_{\Pi}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|(a-b)-y_{1}|+|y_{1}-y_{2}|+\ldots+|y_{k}|\right)}dy_{1}\ldots dy_{k}, $$

where $\Pi=\prod_{i=1}^{N}[x_{i}-\frac{1}{2},x_{i}+\frac{1}{2})$ .

Indeed, using the inequalities

$$ -\frac{1}{l}|x_{i}-x_{i+1}|\leq-\frac{1}{l}|y_{i}-y_{i+1}|+\frac{1}{l}\left(|x_{i}-y_{i}|+|x_{i+1}-y_{i+1}|\right) $$

and $|x_{i}-y_{i}|\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , we conclude that

$$ e^{-\frac{1}{l}|x_{i}-x_{i+1}|}\leq e^{\frac{1}{l}}\cdot e^{-\frac{1}{l}|y_{i}-y_{i+1}|}. $$

Similarly,

$$ e^{-\frac{1}{l}|(a-b)-x_{1}|}\leq e^{\frac{1}{2l}}\cdot e^{-\frac{1}{l}|(a-b)-y_{1}|}\text{ and }e^{-\frac{1}{l}|x_{k}|}\leq e^{\frac{1}{2l}}\cdot e^{-\frac{1}{l}|y_{k}|}. $$

Combining (3.15) and (3.16) and integrating over $\Pi$ we get the inequality (3.14).

Plugging in (3.14) into (3.13), we obtain

$$ Path^{(l)}_{k+1}(a,b)\leq e^{\frac{1}{l}k}\int_{[-N-\frac{1}{2},N+\frac{1}{2})^{k}}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|(a-b)-y_{1}|+|y_{1}-y_{2}|+\ldots+|y_{k}|\right)}dy_{1}\ldots dy_{k}\\
\leq e^{\frac{1}{l}k}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|(a-b)-y_{1}|+|y_{1}-y_{2}|+\ldots+|y_{k}|\right)}dy_{1}\ldots dy_{k}. $$

Replacing the variables $y_{i}$ with $\frac{y_{i}}{l}$ , we see that

$$ Path^{(l)}_{k+1}(a,b)\leq l^{k}e^{\frac{1}{l}k}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}e^{-\left(|\frac{a-b}{l}-y_{1}|+|y_{1}-y_{2}|+\ldots+|y_{k}|\right)}dy_{1}\ldots dy_{k}. $$

Hence, by Lemma 3.3

$$ Path^{(l)}_{k+1}(a,b)\leq l^{k}e^{\frac{1}{l}k}\left(2\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k-1}e^{-\frac{1}{(1+\varepsilon)l}(a-b)}\leq c(l,\varepsilon)^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{(1+\varepsilon)l}(a-b)}, $$

where $c(l,\varepsilon):=le^{\frac{1}{l}}\cdot 2\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}>1$ . Using the inequality $c(l,\varepsilon)^{k}\leq c(l,\varepsilon)^{k+1}$ we get the statement of the lemma. ∎

#### Corollary 3.5.

For fixed $l>0$ there exists a constant $c(l)$ such that for any positive integer $k$ the following inequality holds:

$$ Cyc^{(l)}_{k}:=\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}=1}^{N}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|x_{1}-x_{2}|+\ldots+|x_{k}-x_{1}|\right)}\leq Nc(l)^{k}. $$

#### Proof.

Choose any $\varepsilon>0$ . We rewrite $Cyc^{(l)}_{k}$ as

$$ Cyc^{(l)}_{k}=\sum_{x_{1}=1}^{N}\sum_{x_{2},\ldots,x_{k}=1}^{N}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|x_{1}-x_{2}|+\ldots+|x_{k}-x_{1}|\right)}. $$

Applying Lemma 3.4 to the sums with fixed $x_{1}$ , we get

$$ \sum_{x_{2},\ldots,x_{k}=1}^{N}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\left(|x_{1}-x_{2}|+\ldots+|x_{k}-x_{1}|\right)}\leq c(l,\varepsilon)^{k}. $$

Summing (3.19) over $x_{1}$ and letting $\varepsilon\rightarrow\infty$ , we obtain (3.18). ∎

#### Lemma 3.6.

For any nonnegative integer $k$ and any tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ , every summation graph $G\in Sum(\Gamma)$ is a disjoint union of several connected components $G=P\cup\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}C^{(i)}\right)$ , where $m$ is nonnegative number, $P$ is a path with the ends $p_{0}^{root}$ and $p_{c(root)}^{root}$ and $C^{(i)}$ are cycles. Moreover, for every vertex $v\in V(\Gamma)$ the vertices $p_{0}^{v},\ldots,p_{c(v)}^{v}\in V(G)$ belong to a single component of $G$ .

#### Remark 2.

Note that $m\leq k$ , since $|V(\Gamma)|=k$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the statement by induction on $k$ . The base case of $k=0$ is clear. Fix $k$ and assume that for all $0\leq n<k$ the statement holds for all $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{n}$ . Choose any $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ and any summation graph $G\in Sum(\Gamma)$ . Express $\Gamma$ as $\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}\oplus\Gamma_{2}$ , where $\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{1}}$ , $\Gamma_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{n_{2}}$ and $n_{1}+n_{2}=k-1$ (see Fig. 4). Denote the last child of the root of $\Gamma$ by $w$ . The summation graph $G$ can be naturally split into summation graphs $G_{1}\in Sum(\Gamma_{1})$ and $G_{2}\in Sum(\Gamma_{2})$ , vertex $p_{c(root)}^{root}$ and two other edges (either $\{p_{c(root)-1}^{root},p_{c(root)}^{root}\}$ and $\{p_{0}^{w},p_{c(w)}^{w}\}$ or $\{p_{c(root)-1}^{root},p_{c(w)}^{w}\}$ and $\{p_{0}^{w},p_{c(root)}^{root}\}$ ). Here $root$ refers to the root of $\Gamma$ . Since $n_{1}<k$ and $n_{2}<k$ , the statement of the lemma holds for the graphs $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ (see Fig. 4).

By induction hypothesis, $G_{1}=P_{1}\cup\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m_{1}}C_{1}^{(i)}\right)$ and $G_{2}=P_{2}\cup\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m_{2}}C_{2}^{(i)}\right)$ . The ends of the path $P_{1}$ are $p_{0}^{root}$ and $p_{c(root)-1}^{root}$ , the ends of the path $P_{2}$ are $p_{0}^{w}$ and $p_{c(w)}^{w}$ .

#### Lemma 3.7.

Suppose for some $l>0$ the operator $\mathcal{S}$ has finite $l$ -norm (see (2.3) for the clarification). Then for any positive integer $k$ , any $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ and any $\varepsilon>0$ the matrix $\mathrm{val}(\Gamma)$ has finite $(1+\varepsilon)l$ -norm. Moreover,

$$ \|\mathrm{val}(\Gamma)\|_{(1+\varepsilon)l}\leq N^{k}2^{k}c(l,\varepsilon)^{2k}\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}^{k}. $$

#### Proof.

Recalling the definition of $\mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)$ and using the trivial inequality

$$ |\mathcal{S}_{xy,zt}|\leq e^{-\frac{1}{l}\rho(xy,zt)}\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}, $$

we get, for ane fixed $a$ and $b$ ,

$$ |\mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)|\leq\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}^{k}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\rho(x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}},x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}})}. $$

Since $\rho(xy,zt)=min\{|x-t|+|y-z|,|x-z|+|y-t|\}$ ,

$$ e^{-\frac{1}{l}\rho(xy,zt)}\leq e^{-\frac{1}{l}(|x-t|+|y-z|)}+e^{-\frac{1}{l}(|x-z|+|y-t|)}. $$

Applying this inequality to the product in the RHS of (3.21), removing the parentheses and using the notation from (3.20), we obtain

$$ \prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}\rho(x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}},x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}})}\leq\sum_{G\in Sum(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}s_{G}(\mathbf{x})}. $$

Plugging in (3.22) into (3.21) and changing the order of summation, we get

$$ |\mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)|\leq\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}^{k}\sum_{G\in Sum(\Gamma)}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}s_{G}(\mathbf{x})}. $$

Choose any $G\in Sum(\Gamma)$ . Let $G=P\cup\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}C^{(i)}\right)$ be the representation of $G$ given by Lemma 3.6. Notice that

$$ s_{G}(\mathbf{x})=s_{P}(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_{C^{(i)}}(\mathbf{x}) $$

and each label of $\mathbf{x}$ is included in exactly one summand. Therefore, recalling the definitions of $Path^{(l)}_{k}(a,b)$ and $Cyc^{(l)}_{k}$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}s_{G}(\mathbf{x})}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}s_{P}(\mathbf{x})}\prod_{i=1}^{m}e^{-\frac{1}{l}s_{C^{(i)}}(\mathbf{x})}\\
=Path^{(l)}_{q_{0}}(a,b)\prod_{i=1}^{m}Cyc^{(l)}_{q_{i}}, $$

where $q_{0}=|V(P)|-1$ and $q_{i}=|V(C^{(i)})|$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ . Hence, $\sum_{i=0}^{m}q_{i}=2k$ . Applying Lemma 3.4 and Corollary 3.5 to the RHS of (3.24), we obtain

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}e^{-\frac{1}{l}s_{G}(\mathbf{x})}\leq e^{-\frac{1}{(1+\varepsilon)l}|a-b|}N^{m}c(l,\varepsilon)^{2k}\leq e^{-\frac{1}{(1+\varepsilon)l}|a-b|}N^{k}c(l,\varepsilon)^{2k}. $$

Plugging in (3.25) into (3.23) and recalling that $|Sum(\Gamma)|=2^{k}$ , we get the statement of the lemma. ∎

#### Corollary 3.8.

Under the conditions of Lemma 3.7

$$ \|C_{k}\|_{(1+\varepsilon)l}\leq N^{k}8^{k}c(l,\varepsilon)^{2k}\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}^{k}, $$

where $C_{k}$ is defined by (2.6).

It is sufficient to show that $|\mathcal{T}_{k}|\leq 4^{k}$ . If this inequality holds, (3.26) follows directly from Lemma 3.7.

As mentioned in Section 2.1, one could walk around ordered tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{k}$ starting in the root and making $2k$ steps of two types: going to the first unvisited child if it exists or going to the parent vertex otherwise. Now we prove the main theorem.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.1.

Choose $R(l,\varepsilon)=8c(l,\varepsilon)^{2}c$ . Since $\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}\leq\frac{c}{N}$ , the estimate $\|C_{k}\|_{(1+\varepsilon)l}\leq R(l,\varepsilon)^{k}$ follows from Corollary 3.8. Hence, series (2.5) converges for $|z|^{2}>R(l,\varepsilon)$ and $M(z)$ has finite $(1+\varepsilon)l$ -norm. Moreover,

$$ \|M(z)\|_{(1+\varepsilon)l}\leq|z|^{-1}|1-R(l,\varepsilon)z^{-2}|\text{ for }|z|^{2}>R(l,\varepsilon). $$

By Proposition 3.2, the series (2.5) gives some solution of the equation (1.2). Now we show that $\mathrm{Im}\,M(z)$ is positive for $z\in\mathbb{H}$ . Denote the solution of MDE with positive imaginary part by $\tilde{M}(z)$ . By Proposition 2.1 in [1], $\tilde{M}(z)$ admits a Stieltjes transform representation

$$ \tilde{M}(z)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{V(\mathrm{d}\tau)}{\tau-z},\quad z\in\mathbb{H}. $$

Moreover, $V(\mathrm{d}\tau)$ has compact support, since $\|\mathcal{S}\|_{max}\leq\|\mathcal{S}\|_{l}\leq\frac{c}{N}$ and, hence, $\|\mathcal{S}\|$ is finite. Therefore, there is constant $\tilde{R}$ such that for any $\tau$ in the support of $V$ we have $\left|\frac{1}{\tau-z}\right|\leq\frac{2}{|z|}$ for $|z|>\tilde{R}$ . Thus, there is constant $\tilde{C}$ such that $\|\tilde{M}(z)\|\leq\frac{\tilde{C}}{|z|}$ for $|z|>\tilde{R}$ .

It is easy to see that (3.27) implies that there are constants $R$ and $C$ such that $\|M(z)\|\leq\frac{C}{|z|}$ . Note that we can assume $\tilde{R}=R$ and $\tilde{C}=C$ .

Introduce $U(z)=-zM(z)$ , $\tilde{U}(z)=-z\tilde{M}(z)$ and consider MDE in the form (3.4). Notice that $\|U(z)\|\leq C$ and $\|\tilde{U}(z)\|\leq C$ for $|z|>R$ . Hence, for $|z|>R$ we have

$$ \|U(z)-\tilde{U}(z)\|=|z|^{-2}\|U(z)\mathcal{S}(U(z))-\tilde{U}(z)\mathcal{S}(\tilde{U}(z))\|\\
\leq|z|^{-2}\|(U(z)-\tilde{U}(z))\mathcal{S}(U(z))\|+|z|^{-2}\|\tilde{U(z)}\mathcal{S}(U(z)-\tilde{U}(z))\|\\
\leq|z|^{-2}\cdot 2C\|\mathcal{S}\|\cdot\|U(z)-\tilde{U}(z)\|. $$

Therefore, there is constant $K$ such that $U(z)=\tilde{U}(z)$ for $|z|>K$ . Since both $U(z)$ and $\tilde{U}(z)$ are analytic, $U(z)=\tilde{U}(z)$ in $\mathbb{H}$ .
