## 4 Convergence of the moments of empirical distribution of eigenvalues

In this section we consider Hermitian random matrix $H$ from Section 2.3. All results are obtained under the assumptions (A) and (B).

We are interested in the average moments of empirical distribution $m_{k}^{(N)}:=\mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{k}dL(x)$ for every nonnegative integer $k$ . Notice that

$$ m_{k}^{(N)}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\mathrm{Tr}H^{k}=N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}}. $$

The objective of this section is to prove the following proposition. Theorem 2.2 will be obtained as a corollary.

#### Proposition 4.1.

For any nonnegative integer $k$ :

- • If $k$ is odd,

$$ \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}m_{k}^{(N)}=0. $$

- • If $k$ is even,

$$ \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\left(m_{k}^{(N)}-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{\frac{k}{2}}\right)=0. $$

We start by proving several technical lemmas, the proofs of the Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 2.2 will be given at the end of the section.

### 4.1 Notation

We first introduce some notation. Consider the set $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}=\{\underline{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\mid x_{j}\in[N]\}$ . For every $\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ we construct the semiframe $\mathfrak{F}=\mathfrak{F}(\underline{x})$ with the set of vertices $V(\mathfrak{F})=\{1,2,\ldots,k\}$ , edges $E(\mathfrak{F})=\{\{1,2\},\ldots,\{k-1,k\},\{k,1\}\}$ and the following additional structure. We define the set of proximity edges $Pr(\mathfrak{F})=\{\{i,j\}\mid|x_{i}-x_{j}|\leq(\log N)^{2}\}$ . Let $m=m(\underline{x})$ be such nonnegative integer that the graph with vertices $V(\mathfrak{F})$ and edges $Pr(\mathfrak{F})$ consists of $m+1$ components called proximity components. We denote proximity components by $\mathcal{C}_{0}=\mathcal{C}_{0}(\underline{x}),\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{m}=\mathcal{C}_{m}(\underline{x})$ and order them so that $1=\min(\mathcal{C}_{0})<\min(\mathcal{C}_{1})<\ldots<\min(\mathcal{C}_{m})$ , where $\min(\mathcal{C})$ is meant as the minimum of the set of integers. Finally, we define the graph $\tilde{\Gamma}=\tilde{\Gamma}(\underline{x})$ with the set of vertices $V(\tilde{\Gamma})=\{\mathcal{C}_{0},\ldots,\mathcal{C}_{m}\}$ and $\{\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{j}\}\in E(\tilde{\Gamma})$ iff there is at least one edge between the proximity components $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{j}$ of the semiframe $\mathfrak{F}$ .

We say that edges of the graph $\mathfrak{F}$ connecting components $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{j}$ are associated with the edge $\{\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{j}\}\in E(\tilde{\Gamma})$ .

For $k$ even we call $\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ significant if $m(\underline{x})=\frac{k}{2}$ and for any edge $\{\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{j}\}\in E(\tilde{\Gamma})$ there are exactly two associated edges of semiframe $\mathfrak{F}$ . In this case $|V(\tilde{\Gamma})|=\frac{k}{2}+1$ and $|E(\tilde{\Gamma})|=\frac{k}{2}$ , hence $\tilde{\Gamma}$ is a tree. Define the ordering of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ as follows. Let $\mathcal{C}_{0}$ be the root of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ . If $i<j$ and $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ , $\mathcal{C}_{j}$ have the same parent, they are ordered with respect to the ordering of indices, i.e. $\mathcal{C}_{i}<\mathcal{C}_{j}$ . Hence, $\tilde{\Gamma}\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}$ . Recall the definition of the frame of the ordered tree given in the subsection 2.1. The semiframe $\mathfrak{F}$ is the frame of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ with $p_{0}^{root}=p_{c(root)}^{root}=1$ and vertices of the component $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ are associated with the vertex $\mathcal{C}_{i}\in V(\tilde{\Gamma})$ . The labelling $\mathbf{x}$ of the frame is defined by the components of the array $\underline{x}$ , i.e. for the vertex $p_{i}^{v}=j\in V(\mathfrak{F})$ its label is $x_{i}^{v}=x_{j}$ . Conversely, given the labelling of the frame $\mathbf{x}$ with $x_{0}^{root}=x_{c(root)}^{root}$ , one could obtain the array $\underline{x}$ by ordering the labels of $\mathbf{x}$ with respect to the order of appearance of the vertices in the frame.

Now, consider an ordered tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}$ for some even $k$ . The cyclic frame of the tree $\Gamma$ is the frame of $\Gamma$ with $p_{0}^{root}=p_{c(root)}^{root}$ . We denote the cyclic frame by $\mathcal{F}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ . The labelling of the cyclic frame is any labelling of the frame $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}(\Gamma)$ with $x_{0}^{root}=x_{c(root)}^{root}$ . The set of the labellings of the cyclic frame is denoted by $\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ , i.e.

$$ \mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)=\bigcup_{a\in[N]}\mathcal{X}_{aa}(\Gamma), $$

where $\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)$ is defined in (2.1). Notice that, given a tree $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}$ and the labelling of the cyclic frame $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ , one can define the proximity edges and proximity components on the cyclic frame $\mathcal{F}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ analogously to these structures on the semiframe. We denote the number of proximity components by $m=m(\mathbf{x})$ .

We call $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ significant if for any $v\in V(\Gamma)$ vertices $p_{0}^{v},\ldots,p_{c(v)}^{v}$ form a proximity component. In this case the corresponding $\underline{x}$ is significant and $\tilde{\Gamma}=\Gamma$ . Therefore, for even $k$ we have established the correspondence between the elements of the set ${\{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}\mid\underline{x}\,\text{is significant}\}}$ and the elements of the set

$$ {\{(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\mid\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}},\,\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma),\,\mathbf{x}\,\text{is significant}\}}. $$

Denote the set of partitions of the set $1,\ldots,k$ by $\Pi_{k}$ .

### 4.2 Some estimates on the expectations

#### Lemma 4.2.

For any nonnegative integer $k$ and any array of indices $\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ with $m=m(\underline{x})\geq\frac{k}{2}$ there is a constant $c$ such that:

- • If $\underline{x}$ is not significant,

$$ |\mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}}|\leq|\Pi_{k}|c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}. $$

(4.2)

- • If $\underline{x}$ is significant,

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}}-\prod_{e\in E(\tilde{\Gamma})}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}\right|\leq\left|\Pi_{k}\right|c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}, $$

(4.3) where $\mathbf{x}$ is corresponding labelling of the frame of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ .

#### Proof.

We express the expectation of products of random variables through their cumulants using the relation

$$ \mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}}=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{k}}\prod_{B\in\pi}\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}\mid i\in B), $$

where $x_{k+1}:=x_{1}$ (see Appendix A in [3]).

Consider one summand of this sum with fixed $\pi\in\Pi_{k}$ . If there is $B\in\pi$ such that $|B|=1$ , then $\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}\mid i\in B)=\mathbb{E}w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}=0$ , where $B=\{i\}$ . Hence, this summand is $0$ . Otherwise, by (2.9),

$$ |\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}\mid i\in B)|\leq\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T_{B})}|\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}},w_{x_{j}x_{j+1}})|, $$

where $T_{B}$ is the minimal spanning tree of the complete graph with the set of vertices $B$ and edge length $d(\{i,j\})=\rho(x_{i}x_{i+1},x_{j}x_{j+1})$ .

Sence semiframe $\mathfrak{F}$ is a cycle, it is connected. Therefore, the graph $\tilde{\Gamma}(\underline{x})$ is connected and has $m+1$ vertices. Hence, it has at least $m$ edges. Consider the case, where $\underline{x}$ is not significant. Since $m\geq\frac{k}{2}$ , there is at least one edge of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ with a single associated edge of semiframe $\mathfrak{F}$ . Denote this edge by $\{i_{0},i_{0}+1\}$ . Let $B_{0}\in\pi$ be such partition set, that $i_{0}\in B_{0}$ . Since $|B_{0}|\geq 2$ , there is such $j_{0}\in B_{0}$ that $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ is the edge of the minimal spanning tree $T_{B_{0}}$ . The edges $\{i_{0},i_{0}+1\}$ and $\{j_{0},j_{0}+1\}$ are associated with different edges of $\tilde{\Gamma}(\underline{x})$ . Therefore, either vertices $i_{0}$ , $j_{0}$ or vertices $i_{0}+1$ , $j_{0}+1$ belong to different proximity components. Likewise, either vertices $i_{0}$ , $j_{0}+1$ or vertices $i_{0}+1$ , $j_{0}$ belong to different proximity components. Hence,

$$ \rho(x_{i_{0}}x_{i_{0}+1},x_{j_{0}}x_{j_{0}+1})=\min\{|x_{i_{0}}-x_{j_{0}}|+|x_{i_{0}+1}-x_{j_{0}+1}|,|x_{i_{0}}-x_{j_{0}+1})|+|x_{i_{0}+1}-x_{j_{0}}|\}\\
\geq(\log N)^{2}. $$

Using (2.8) and (4.6), we get

$$ \left|\kappa(w_{x_{i_{0}}x_{i_{0}+1}},w_{x_{j_{0}}x_{j_{0}+1}})\right|\leq ce^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}. $$

For each $B\in\pi$ and each edge $\{i,j\}$ of $T_{B}$ , such that $\{i,j\}\neq\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ , estimate (2.8) implies that

$$ \left|\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}},w_{x_{j}x_{j+1}})\right|\leq c. $$

Applying (4.7), (4.8) and (4.5) to the summand for $\pi$ in the RHS of (4.4), we obtain

$$ \left|\prod_{B\in\pi}\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}\mid i\in B)\right|\leq\left(\prod_{B\in\pi}c^{|B|-1}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}\leq c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}. $$

Summing over $\pi\in\Pi_{k}$ , we get the estimate (4.2).

Now, if $\underline{x}$ is significant, consider the partition $\pi^{\prime}\in\Pi_{k}$ , such that $i$ and $j$ belong to the same set of $\pi^{\prime}$ iff $\{i,i+1\}$ and $\{j,j+1\}$ are associated with the same edge of $\tilde{\Gamma}(\underline{x})$ . Then $|B|=2$ for any $B\in\pi^{\prime}$ . Hence, any other other partition $\pi\in\Pi_{k}$ , $\pi\neq\pi^{\prime}$ contains either $B\in\pi$ with $|B|=1$ , or $B_{0}\in\pi$ such that edges $\{i,i+1\}$ with $i\in B_{0}$ are not associated with the same edge of $\tilde{\Gamma}(\underline{x})$ . In the former case, the summand of (4.4) with such $\pi$ is 0. In the latter case, one could find the edge $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ of $T_{B_{0}}$ such that $\{i_{0},i_{0}+1\}$ and $\{j_{0},j_{0}+1\}$ are associated with different edges of $\tilde{\Gamma}(\underline{x})$ . Hence, the estimate (4.9) holds for such $\pi$ .

Since the entries $w_{yz}$ are centered, $\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}},w_{x_{j}x_{j+1}})=\mathbb{E}w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}w_{x_{j}x_{j+1}}$ . Therefore,

$$ \prod_{B\in\pi^{\prime}}\kappa(w_{x_{i}x_{i+1}}\mid i\in B)=\prod_{B=\{i_{B},j_{B}\}\in\pi^{\prime}}\kappa(w_{x_{i_{B}}x_{i_{B}+1}},w_{x_{j_{B}}x_{j_{B}+1}})\\
=\prod_{B=\{i_{B},j_{B}\}\in\pi^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{i_{B}}x_{i_{B}+1}}w_{x_{j_{B}}x_{j_{B}+1}}=\prod_{e\in E(\tilde{\Gamma})}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}, $$

where the last identity follows from one-to-one correspondence between the partition sets $B\in\pi^{\prime}$ and edges of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ .

Separating $\pi^{\prime}$ partition in (4.4) and evaluating by (4.10), then applying (4.9) to remaining summands on the RHS of (4.4), we get the estimate (4.3).

∎

#### Lemma 4.3.

For any even nonnegative integer $k$ , any $\Gamma\in T_{\frac{k}{2}}$ and any labelling of the cyclic frame $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ with $m=m(\mathbf{x})\geq\frac{k}{2}$ such that $\mathbf{x}$ is not significant, we have

$$ \left|\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}\right|\leq c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

If for any edge $e\in E(\Gamma)$ the edges $\{p_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}},p_{0}^{e_{+}}\}$ and $\{p_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}},p_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}\}$ are associated with a single edge of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ , then the vertices associated with the same vertex of $\Gamma$ belong to the same proximity component (this can be proved similarly to the Lemma 3.6). Hence, either $m<\frac{k}{2}$ or $\mathbf{x}$ is significant, which is excluded by the conditions of the lemma.

Thus, there is such edge $\hat{e}\in E(\Gamma)$ that the edges $\{p_{n(\hat{e}_{+})-1}^{\hat{e}_{-}},p_{0}^{\hat{e}_{+}}\}$ and $\{p_{c(\hat{e}_{+})}^{\hat{e}_{+}},p_{n(\hat{e}_{+})}^{\hat{e}_{-}}\}$ are associated with different edges of $\tilde{\Gamma}$ .

We estimate the expectations using the assumption on the decay of cumulants. More precisely, for the edge $\hat{e}$

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(\hat{e}_{+})-1}^{\hat{e}_{-}}x_{0}^{\hat{e}_{+}}}w_{x_{c(\hat{e}_{+})}^{\hat{e}_{+}}x_{n(\hat{e}_{+})}^{\hat{e}_{-}}}\right|\leq ce^{-\frac{1}{l}\rho(x_{n(\hat{e}_{+})-1}^{\hat{e}_{-}}x_{0}^{\hat{e}_{+}},x_{c(\hat{e}_{+})}^{\hat{e}_{+}}x_{n(\hat{e}_{+})}^{\hat{e}_{-}})}\leq ce^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}. $$

For any other edge $e\in E(\Gamma)$ such that $e\neq\hat{e}$ , we have

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}\right|\leq c. $$

Hence, the inequality (4.11) holds.

∎

#### Lemma 4.4.

For any nonnegative $k$

$$ \left|\{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}\mid m(\underline{x})<\frac{k}{2}\}\right|\leq c(k)N^{\frac{k+1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}, $$

where $c(k)$ only depends on $k$ .

#### Proof.

Denote $l=\left\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\right\rfloor$ . Let $\tilde{c}(k)$ be the number of partitions of the set $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ into no more than $l$ subsets. Fix some partition $\pi$ and consider the subset $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{\pi}$ of $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ , consisting of such $\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ that for each proximity component of $\mathfrak{F}(\underline{x})$ , its vertices form the subsets of partition $\pi$ .

Choose a subset $A\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}$ such that $|A|=l$ and $A\cap B$ is not empty for each subset $B$ in $\pi$ . There are $N^{l}$ ways to choose indices $x_{i}\in[N]$ , $i\in A$ . If $A\neq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ , there is $j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\setminus A$ such that $j$ is connected by proximity edge to some $i\in A$ . Since $i$ and $j$ are connected, $|x_{i}-x_{j}|<(\log N)^{2}$ . Hence, there are at most $2(\log N)^{2}$ allowed values of $x_{j}$ . Repeating this choice until all $x_{i}$ are fixed for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ , we get

$$ |\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{\pi}|\leq N^{l}(2(\log N)^{2})^{k-l}\leq 2^{k}N^{\frac{k+1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}. $$

Therefore, the inequality (4.12) holds with $c(k)=2^{k}\tilde{c}(k)$ .

∎

### 4.3 Proofs of Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 2.2

#### Proof of the Proposition 4.1.

We decompose the set $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ into the union of three sets $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}=\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{1}\cup\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{2}\cup\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{1} \displaystyle=\{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}\mid m(\underline{x})<\frac{k}{2}\}; \displaystyle\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{2} \displaystyle=\{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}\mid m(\underline{x})\geq\frac{k}{2},\,\underline{x}\,\text{is not significant}\}; \displaystyle\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3} \displaystyle=\{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}\mid\underline{x}\,\text{is significant}\}. $$

Note that this union is disjoint, since $m(\underline{x})=\frac{k}{2}$ for significant $\underline{x}$ . Recall the empirical moments from (4.1). We decompose $m_{k}^{(N)}$ into three sums in accordance with the decomposition of $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ , i.e. $m_{k}^{(N)}=S_{1}+S_{2}+S_{3}$ , where

$$ S_{i}=N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{i}}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}} $$

for any $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ .

In the sum $S_{1}$ we estimate each summand using Hölder inequality as follows:

$$ |\mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}}|\leq\left(\mathbb{E}|w_{x_{1}x_{2}}|^{k}\cdot\ldots\cdot\mathbb{E}|w_{x_{k}x_{1}}|^{k}\right)^{\frac{1}{k}}\leq\mu_{k}, $$

where $\mu_{k}$ is the constant from (2.7). By Lemma 4.4, $|\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{1}|\leq c(k)N^{\frac{k+1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}$ . Hence,

$$ |S_{1}|\leq N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}c(k)N^{\frac{k+1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}\mu_{k}=c(k)\mu_{k}N^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}\rightarrow 0, $$

as $N\rightarrow\infty$ for any fixed $k$ .

Since $x_{i}\in[N]$ for any $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ , $|\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{2}|\leq N^{k}$ . Applying Lemma 4.2 to each summand of $S_{2}$ , we get

$$ |S_{2}|\leq N^{k}|\Pi_{k}|c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}\rightarrow 0, $$

as $N\rightarrow\infty$ , since $l$ is fixed and $N$ -independent.

If $k$ is odd, the set $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3}$ is empty. Hence, $S_{3}=0$ and $m_{k}^{(N)}\rightarrow 0$ , as $N\rightarrow\infty$ .

If $k$ is even, from (2.6) we have

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,C_{\frac{k}{2}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}}\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathrm{val}(\Gamma). $$

Recalling the definition of $\mathrm{val}(\Gamma)$

$$ \mathrm{val}_{ab}(\Gamma)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{ab}(\Gamma)}\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}} $$

and plugging it into (4.13), we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,C_{\frac{k}{2}}=N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)}\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}. $$

Consider the set $\mathsf{X}^{(k)}=\{(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\mid\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}},\,\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)\}$ and decompose it into disjoint union $\mathsf{X}^{(k)}=\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{1}\cup\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{2}\cup\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{3}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{1} \displaystyle=\{(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\in\mathsf{X}^{(k)}\mid m(\mathbf{x})<\frac{k}{2}\}; \displaystyle\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{2} \displaystyle=\{(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\in\mathsf{X}^{(k)}\mid m(\mathbf{x})\geq\frac{k}{2},\,\mathbf{x}\,\text{is not significant}\}; \displaystyle\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{3} \displaystyle=\{(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\in\mathsf{X}^{(k)}\mid\mathbf{x}\,\text{is significant}\}. $$

The sum (4.14) can be decomposed accordingly as $\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}\,C_{\frac{k}{2}}=\hat{S}_{1}+\hat{S}_{2}+\hat{S}_{3}$ , where for any $i\in\{1,2,3\}$

$$ \hat{S}_{i}=N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\in\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{i}}\prod_{e\in E(\Gamma)}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}. $$

Notice that for any fixed $\Gamma\in\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}$ the elements of the set $\mathcal{X}_{cyc}(\Gamma)$ are in one-to-one correspondence with the elements of the set $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}$ . Thus, according to Lemma 4.4,

$$ |\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{1}|\leq|\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}|c(k)N^{\frac{k+1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}. $$

By Hölder inequality, for each $(\Gamma,\mathbf{x})\in\mathsf{X}^{(k)}$ and each $e\in E(\Gamma)$

$$ |\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}|\leq\mu_{2}. $$

Applying (4.15) and (4.16) to the sum $\hat{S}_{1}$ , we get

$$ |\hat{S}_{1}|\leq N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}|\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}|c(k)N^{\frac{k+1}{2}}(\log N)^{2k}\mu_{2}^{\frac{k}{2}}\rightarrow 0, $$

as $N\rightarrow\infty$ .

Applying Lemma 4.3 to each summand of $\hat{S}_{2}$ and using inequality $|\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{2}|\leq|\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}|N^{k}$ , we obtain

$$ |\hat{S}_{2}|\leq N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}|\mathcal{T}_{\frac{k}{2}}|N^{k}c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}\rightarrow 0, $$

as $N\rightarrow\infty$ .

This proves that

$$ m_{k}^{(N)}-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{\frac{k}{2}}=S_{3}-\hat{S}_{3}+o(1)\text{ as }N\rightarrow\infty. $$

Since there is correspondence between the sets $\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3}$ and $\mathsf{X}^{(k)}_{3}$ , the difference $S_{3}-\hat{S}_{3}$ can be estimated using Lemma 4.2:

$$ \left|S_{3}-\hat{S}_{3}\right|\leq N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}\sum_{\underline{x}\in\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3}}\left|\mathbb{E}w_{x_{1}x_{2}}\ldots w_{x_{k-1}x_{k}}w_{x_{k}x_{1}}-\prod_{e\in E(\tilde{\Gamma})}\mathbb{E}w_{x_{n(e_{+})-1}^{e_{-}}x_{0}^{e_{+}}}w_{x_{c(e_{+})}^{e_{+}}x_{n(e_{+})}^{e_{-}}}\right|\\
\leq N^{-\frac{k}{2}-1}\left|\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3}\right|\left|\Pi_{k}\right|c^{k}e^{-\frac{1}{l}(\log N)^{2}}. $$

Applying inequality $\left|\mathbb{X}^{(k)}_{3}\right|\leq N^{k}$ , we obtain that $\left|S_{3}-\hat{S}_{3}\right|\rightarrow 0$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$ . Hence, $m_{k}^{(N)}-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{\frac{k}{2}}\rightarrow 0$ .

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 2.2.

Armed with Proposition 4.1, this proof is fairly standard. Here we follow the argument in Section 2.1.2 of [2]. From Proposition 2.1 in [1] we know that $\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}M(z)$ is Stieltjes transform of some measure $\mu_{N}$ for each $N$ and measures $\mu_{N}$ are supported on the set $[-B,B]$ for some constant $B$ . Notice that, since $\mu_{N}$ is a probability measure,

$$ \left|\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{k}\right|=\left|\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}x^{2k}\mu_{N}(\mathrm{d}x)\right|\leq B^{2k}. $$

Consider the integral

$$ \int\limits_{|x|>(B+1)^{2}}|x|^{k}\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)\leq\frac{1}{(B+1)^{2k}}\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}}x^{2k}\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)=\frac{m_{2k}^{(N)}}{(B+1)^{2k}}. $$

Since $m_{2k}^{(N)}=(m_{2k}^{(N)}-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{k}(z))+\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{k}(z)$ and $|m_{2k}^{(N)}-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{k}(z)|\rightarrow 0$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$ (see Proposition 4.1), we have

$$ \limsup_{N\rightarrow\infty}\int\limits_{|x|>(B+1)^{2}}|x|^{k}\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)=\limsup_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{k}(z)}{(B+1)^{2k}}\leq\left(\frac{B}{B+1}\right)^{2k}. $$

Notice that LHS is increasing in $k$ and RHS goes to $0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$ . Hence,

$$ \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\int\limits_{|x|>(B+1)^{2}}|x|^{k}\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)=0. $$

Fix any $z\in\mathbb{H}$ such that $|z|>(B+1)^{2}$ . Denote $(B+1)^{2}$ by $D$ . Since $(x-z)^{-1}$ is a bounded function of $x$ , (4.18) for $k=0$ implies that

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}S^{(N)}(z)-\int\limits_{-D}^{D}\frac{\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)}{x-z}\right|\rightarrow 0\text{ as }N\rightarrow\infty. $$

Then $-\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^{k}z^{-k-1}$ converges to $(x-z)^{-1}$ uniformly in $x$ on $[-D,D]$ . Hence,

$$ \left|\int\limits_{-D}^{D}\frac{\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)}{x-z}-\int\limits_{-D}^{D}\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^{k}z^{-k-1}\right)\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)\right|\rightarrow 0, $$

uniformly in $N$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ .

Notice that

$$ \int\limits_{-D}^{D}\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^{k}z^{-k-1}\right)\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)=-\sum_{k=0}^{n}\left(\int\limits_{-D}^{D}x^{k}\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)\right)z^{-k-1}. $$

Therefore, (4.18) implies that

$$ \left|\int\limits_{-D}^{D}\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n}x^{k}z^{-k-1}\right)\mathbb{E}L^{(N)}(\mathrm{d}x)-\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n}m_{k}^{(N)}z^{-k-1}\right)\right|\rightarrow 0, $$

as $N\rightarrow\infty$ . By Proposition 4.1,

$$ \left|\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n}m_{k}^{(N)}z^{-k-1}\right)-\left(-\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}k=0\\
k\text{ even}\end{subarray}}^{n}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{\frac{k}{2}}z^{-k-1}\right)\right|\rightarrow 0\text{ as }N\rightarrow\infty. $$

From (4.17) we have

$$ \left|\left(-\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}k=0\\
k\text{ even}\end{subarray}}^{n}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{\frac{k}{2}}z^{-k-1}\right)-\left(-\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}k=0\\
k\text{ even}\end{subarray}}^{\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}C_{\frac{k}{2}}z^{-k-1}\right)\right|\rightarrow 0, $$

uniformly in $N$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ .

Combining (4.19), (4.20), (4.21), (4.22), (4.23) and letting $n\rightarrow\infty$ , $N\rightarrow\infty$ , we get

$$ \left|\mathbb{E}S^{(N)}(z)-\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}M(z)\right|\rightarrow 0, $$

as $N\rightarrow\infty$ for $|z|>D$ .

It is easy to show that (4.24) holds for all $z\in\mathbb{H}$ by applying Montel’s theorem to Stieltjes transforms and functions $\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}M(z)$ . ∎

Abstract Introduction  A range of quantitative studies has identified intimate partner violence (IPV) as a risk factor for perinatal mental health conditions, and adverse obstetric and child outcomes. Rich qualitative literature has explored women’s experiences of both perinatal mental health and IPV in the African region, in isolation. However, qualitative findings about relationships between the two are less widely reported. Methods  We searched systematically for qualitative studies exploring women’s experiences of IPV and perinatal mental health conditions in the African region up to 16/09/2024. We searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, LILACS, ScieELO, Wiley online library, Cochrane, 3ie, Google Scholar, and included studies’ reference lists. We used a piloted form to extract qualitative data before qualitatively analysing the findings using reflexive thematic analysis. We assessed included studies’ risk of bias using the Critical Appraisal Skills Program qualitative reviews checklist and registered the protocol prospectively on the PROSPERO database (CRD42022278592). Results  Of 4105 identified studies, 22 met inclusion criteria. The over-arching theme was cycles of suffering. Four intersecting sub-themes were socio-cultural norms, perinatal abuse, dependence and vulnerability, and foci of distress. Different forms of interpersonal violence perpetrated by partners and family members interacted with the range of women’s experiences of structural violence. Economic dependence on partners heightened perinatal vulnerability and distress, especially in women with additional vulnerabilities. Socio-cultural norms regarding gender inequity contributed to normalisation of violence and women’s sense of entrapment. A range of perinatal psychological and somatic symptoms was linked to IPV; spirituality was a key coping strategy. Where service provider perspectives were reported, lack of relevant training and resources were barriers to identification of and response to the mental health impacts of perinatal IPV.

Perinatal mental health impacts of intimate partner violence in the African region: a systematic review and qualitative metasynthesis

Introduction Violence against women is a global public health crisis ‘of pandemic proportions’ [1]. Intimate partner violence (IPV) comprises behaviour by a current or ex-partner causing physical, sexual or psychological harm [2]. Global data indicate that 27% of women worldwide experience IPV in their lifetime, and this risk is higher in the Afri­ can region [3]. Demographic and health surveys (DHS) in 27 countries in the African region report a median 25% prevalence of past-year IPV among married or cohabiting women aged 15 to 24 years, alone [4].

Risk factors for IPV exposure operate at individual, relationship, community, and societal levels. Individual risk factors include limited access to education or paid employment and previous experience of abuse [5]. At the relationship level, substantial age gaps between partners appear to increase the risk of IPV whilst at community and societal levels, IPV is more prevalent in settings of higher gender inequity [4]. Changing physical, psycho­ logical, and social needs during the perinatal period (from conception to 12 months post-partum) interact with these factors to increase risk [5, 6].

IPV is an established social determinant of health, with impacts on women and children. The bidirectional rela­ tionship between IPV and mental health is well-estab­ lished. IPV survivors commonly experience depression [7], anxiety symptoms, harmful alcohol use [8], selfharm, suicidal thoughts and attempts [9], while people with mental health conditions also experience excess IPV victimisation [7, 10]. Pathways between mental health and IPV include relationship quality and interpersonal conflict, and through shared structural determinants such as poverty, gender inequity and lack of social sup­ port [11]. As an independent risk factor for both expe­ riencing and perpetrating IPV, children’s experiences of witnessing household IPV appeaexposure, outcome). Full text articles of studies flagr to perpetuate the cycle of intergenerational violence [12, 13].

The perinatal period is a time of biological, psycho­ logical and social transition in a woman’s life. A grow­ ing body of evidence has identified multifactorial risk and protective factors for mental health conditions during the perinatal period and their intergenerational consequences [14–16]. Individual-level risk factors include genetic predisposition, and IPV, while wider social determinants include restrictive gender norms,

limited availability and access to health care, expo­ sure to armed conflict and climate events [17]. Con­ versely, a randomised controlled trial (RCT) in South Africa identified a lower prevalence of postpartum depression among the relatively small proportion of women who were accompanied to antenatal care and childbirth by the father of their baby [18]. A systematic review of common perinatal mental health conditions in low- and lower-middle income countries found that risk was amplified in the presence of multiple risks [19], highlighting the importance of intervention for modifiable factors.

Women experiencing IPV during the perinatal period experience the same adverse health impacts as women outside this timeframe, with additional risks to the pregnancy or infant [20, 21]. Antenatal IPV is associated with adverse obstetric outcomes, including low birthweight, preterm birth, miscarriage, and child mortality [6]. A meta-analysis also reported associa­ tions between IPV prior to pregnancy and both prema­ ture delivery and low birthweight, among studies with substantial heterogeneity [22]. Both IPV and perinatal mental health conditions can reduce women’s readi­ ness and ability to access healthcare, including antena­ tal services and skilled care during delivery, impacting health outcomes further and limiting opportunities for intervention [23]. Understanding the perinatal mental health impacts of IPV can optimise interventions and service designs, to safeguard the physical and mental health and safety of women and their children.

Rationale Qualitative methods are particularly powerful for illu­ minating women’s perspectives and lived experience, deepening our understanding of quantitative associa­ tions. Despite rich, distinct, bodies of qualitative lit­ erature exploring perinatal mental health and IPV in Africa in isolation, relationships between the two in the region are far less studied.

Objectives We aimed to synthesise qualitative evidence for relationships between perinatal mental health and IPV exposure in Africa, through a qualitative meta-synthesis.

Conclusions  Relationships between perinatal mental health and IPV in the African region are complex. Interpersonal and structural factors reinforce harmful gender norms and normalise IPV, increasing women’s distress and risk of perinatal mental health conditions. While antenatal care represents an opportunity for identification and response, disrupting cycles of suffering to improve women’s mental health requires broader, culturally sensitive, multisectoral programmes addressing pervasive IPV and structural violence. Keywords  Intimate partner violence, Perinatal mental health, Sub-Saharan Africa, Qualitative research, Meta-synthesis

Materials and methods Eligibility criteria We sought studies enrolling female participants living in any sub-Saharan African country who were or had been pregnant (population) and experienced IPV (exposure), where mental health impacts were mentioned (outcome). Studies of female participants aged 10 years and older were eligible (to capture evidence for IPV within child marriage), with no upper age limits. We did not exclude papers based on the duration or outcome of pregnancy, nor duration or type of IPV exposure. IPV was the expo­ sure of interest but we planned to note evidence for wider domestic violence (perpetrated by adult, non-partner family or household members), where mentioned. Given our focus on qualitative evidence, we sought studies reporting a range of outcomes, including common men­ tal disorder, severe mental illness, substance use disorder, neurodevelopmental, cognitive, eating, and personality disorder symptoms, and bodily distress including somatic and functional symptoms. Eligible studies were required to report at least some qualitative findings, such as from interviews, focus group discussions, or free-text survey responses.

Information sources We searched 10 databases: Medline (PubMed), 3ie Impact Repository, Cochrane, Wiley Online Library, SciELO, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Google Scholar, and Embase. We also searched the reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews, and checked references made by relevant quantitative studies to linked qualitative research.

Search strategy We combined search terms for “pregnancy” and “sub- Saharan Africa” (population), “intimate partner violence” (exposure), “mental health conditions” (outcome) and “qualitative methods” (design), using Boolean operators (see Supplementary Table 1). We searched for English language results on 21/08/2023 and updated the search for more recent publications on 16/09/2024.

Selection process We downloaded all search results to the online platform, Rayyan, and electronically removed all duplicates [24]. Our team of five researchers then screened the titles and abstracts of all results against the inclusion criteria, not­ ing any reasons for exclusion using a hierarchical system (region, study design, population, exposure, outcome). Full text articles of studies flagged as potentially eligible were then checked for final eligibility. Cases of disagree­ ment were screened at the full text level by one reviewer (AK) and discussed with a second (RK). A random

sample of 20% of results was second-screened by a differ­ ent reviewer, to quantify screening reliability.

Data collection process Once identified, four reviewers extracted data from all included full text articles into a piloted spreadsheet.

Data items General extraction fields comprised first author, pub­ lication year, country, study setting, participant char­ acteristics, sample size, demographic characteristics, method of IPV ascertainment, IPV time-frame, data col­ lection method, qualitative analysis method, methods for ensuring rigour, methods for ensuring participant safety, and details of any related qualitative work pub­ lished elsewhere. For mixed methods studies, we noted details of any linked quantitative work. For each paper, we extracted raw qualitative data (participant quota­ tions or author statements) pertaining to the relationship between women’s perinatal mental health and exposure to IPV.

Study risk of bias assessment Authors extracting data performed risk of bias assess­ ments of all included papers using the Critical Appraisal Skills Program (CASP) qualitative studies checklist [25].

Synthesis methods We uploaded qualitative data to NVIVO [26] to facili­ tate reflexive thematic analysis [27] by three researchers (MCH, AK and RK). This analytical approach employed subjectivity and reflexivity for ‘meaning making’ across included studies in light of each paper’s individual con­ text. MCH, AK and RK initially immersed in the data and assigned codes based on individual interpretations. Authors then discussed codes, to group related concepts into descriptive themes, in an iterative process referring back to the wider literature.

Rigour We remained reflexive throughout; each author inde­ pendently extracted data from studies whilst remining mindful of their background and personal circumstances. During triangulation we utilised diverse lived experiences of BK as an Ethiopian researcher, AK as a violence spe­ cialist and RK as a clinical academic psychiatrist. Synthe­ sising and discussing codes independently generated by authors from diverse backgrounds helped to ground our results in the data.

We remained mindful of how intersectional personal experience impacted each researcher’s unconscious bias, especially among team members living outside the Afri­ can region. As a meta-synthesis we did not undertake additional respondent validation beyond that conducted

in the individual studies. Additionally, we recognised that whilst responses were reported in English, many inter­ views had been translated from local dialects, in which spoken language often conveys deeper, culturally situated meanings which cannot always be accurately translated.

We registered our study protocol on the PROSPERO international prospective register of systematic reviews (#CRD42022278592) on 14/01/2022. We report our find­ ings in accordance with PRISMA (preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses) guide­ lines [28]; see Supplementary Table 2 for the PRISMA checklist.

Results Study selection Our systematic searches yielded 4089 results from 10 databases plus an additional 16 papers from alternative sources, of which 48 were duplicates. After screening titles and abstracts, we identified 130 potentially eligible papers, for full text screening against inclusion crite­ ria. We ultimately included 22 papers in our qualitative

meta-synthesis. The flow of studies through the selection process is presented in Fig. 1.

Study characteristics The 22 included studies (see Table  1) were conducted across eight countries, predominantly South Africa and Ethiopia (both n = 7). Other countries were Uganda (n = 3), Kenya (n = 2), Zambia, Ghana, and Benin (all n = 1). Sample sizes ranged from four to 273 (median: 20); most studies enrolled participants in community antena­ tal care services.

Of the 22 included papers, only two explicitly set out to study the impact of IPV on perinatal mental health in the African region [29, 30]. In the remaining 20 studies, impacts of IPV on perinatal mental health were identified while exploring broader topics of perinatal mental health, pregnancy and motherhood, or IPV in Africa. Data col­ lection was predominantly through semi-structured interviews; five studies conducted focus group discus­ sions and one study qualitatively analysed retrospective case notes.

Perinatal abuse Abuse was predominantly perpetrated by partners, but harm from women’s parents [34, 40] and in-laws [31, 47, 48] was also reported. Across studies, severe physical violence was described most often (for example, use of weapons, kicking in the abdomen, head-butting, loss of teeth), in South Africa [31, 33, 47], Zambia [46], Ethiopia [37, 48], Kenya [39], Uganda [40], Benin [42], and Ghana [50]. Perinatal sexual IPV was reported less often, but where it was, entailed lack of choice about sexual activ­ ity late in pregnancy and early post-partum [47, 48, 50]. Women described partners preventing them from leaving [33, 38] and monitoring their movements at home [48]. In Ethiopia [48] and Ghana [50], men controlled women’s access to and use of contraception, conflict about which sometimes progressed to physical or sexual IPV. Harm­ ing women through their children, via physical violence, threatening to take children to another wife, or obstruct­ ing children’s HIV treatment, was reported in Ethiopia [48], Uganda [45], and Zambia [46].

Dependence and vulnerability In South Africa [33], Zambia [46], Ethiopia [35, 36], Uganda [45], and Ghana [50], increased dependence on

partners in the perinatal period was considered central to the mental health impact of IPV on women:

I know he increased his abuse because he knows that I don’t have anybody to protect me and he knows that I need support in this period. It’s me who suffers with the pregnancy [starts crying]. If I had not been pregnant, I would not have been vulnerable like this. Ethiopia [36].

This dependence was further exacerbated in those women with additional vulnerabilities. Factors mak­ ing women more vulnerable to abuse included adoles­ cence [33, 39–41], disability [44], perinatal losses [42], HIV infection [39, 46], and commercial sex work [39]. Adolescents in Uganda faced community stigma, paren­ tal and partner rejection, and hostility from healthcare professionals [40, 41]. Routine mistreatment sometimes extended to physical violence from family and partners, neglect of their needs, such as denial of food and bed­ ding, and being forced into marriage [40, 41, 47] or ter­ mination of pregnancy [34].

Women with disabilities in Ethiopia described sexual violence victimisation due to their physical vulnerability, leading to pregnancy and forced marriage [44]. In Benin, physical IPV was linked to marital and family tensions around pregnancy loss, including accusations of infidel­ ity and stressors from meeting healthcare costs [42]. In Zambia, HIV closely intersected with IPV [46]. Fear of IPV and abandonment prevented women from disclosing

their HIV status, while women in serodiscordant rela­ tionships described emotional abuse around their status. Women described both being accused of promiscuity and their HIV status being used to justify their partner’s infidelity.

Studies identified women’s financial inability to meet their own and their children’s basic needs, as central to the mental health impacts of IPV. Distress from lack of funds to access healthcare was raised in Ghana, for treat­ ment following physical IPV [50], in South Africa, for HIV and antenatal care [32], and in Ethiopia for the baby, if they became ill [35]. In Kenya [39] and South Africa [32], adequate shelter was a source of anxiety. In rural Ethiopia, martial conflict around insufficient food [37], exacerbated by pregnancy [35] and partner alcohol use [30], were factors linking IPV and women’s poor mental health. Worsening of the severity of IPV by men’s drink­ ing, which in turn worsened women’s mental health, was raised in Ethiopia [30, 38, 48], South Africa [31, 43, 47], and Ghana [50].

Socio-cultural norms Certain cultural practices were highlighted as exacer­ bating women’s entrapment and distress. In Ethiopia, traditional avoidance of socialising in the third trimes­ ter caused isolation and limited women’s access to sup­ port [38]. The practice of postnatal confinement was also linked to emotional symptoms in women with existing vulnerabilities [35]. In Ghana, patrilineal kinship entails children belonging to their father, impacting women’s ability to leave:

He treated me like a slave that is of no use … I almost died [silent] I felt seriously ill … I was suffer­ ing but decided not to leave because of my children. Ghana [50].

Patriarchal norms further exacerbating perinatal IPV included rejection and hostility towards female infants [48], unequal consequences for male and female adoles­ cents following conception [41], opposition to women’s financial agency [39], disempowerment [37], patrilineal cultural practices [50], and loss of family support follow­ ing marriage:

When I report this matter to my family they would tell me that he is my husband and he has paid the dowry therefore there is nothing that they could do. I have told myself that I am all alone in this matter. There is no one who cares about me. South Africa [31].

Researchers often raised the mental health impact of entrenched patriarchal norms, although women did not often challenge them explicitly: [30, 31, 34, 47]

He says I’m a woman and I must do it [housework and childcare]. I said, ‘But I’m a person also, I’m not just a woman’. South Africa [34].

Foci of distress In Uganda and South Africa, loss of the freedom and agency to pursue an education following pregnancy was a source of bereavement [34, 41] to women. Feelings of hopelessness towards the pregnancy, feeling forced to seek termination or adoption, and feeling ‘colonised by the baby’ were linked to suicidal thoughts and acts [34]. Women expressed preoccupation with their deaths, dur­ ing childbirth [37], from IPV [30], or suicide:

The only thing they see in their minds is death. You feel that you need to take poison or get a rope and go hang yourself. Those are the things that cross your mind. Kenya [49].

A common source of women’s distress was men’s failure to meet their (sometimes, culturally-mandated) expecta­ tions of practical and emotional support during and after the pregnancy, in South Africa [31, 33, 34], Zambia [46], Ethiopia [35], Kenya [39], Uganda [41], and Ghana [50]. This led to feelings of dissonance, between experiences and expectations:

One thing that pains me the most is that the father of my child never comes to check on us. That’s what I am always worried about. He does make phone calls saying he would come over for the weekend, but he never does that… the child was born in July when it’s usually very cold. South Africa [31].

Women also expressed dissonance from comparison of their circumstances to those of peers (feeling “the last out of all your neighbours” [37]. Dissonance compounded women’s feelings of shame [34, 48, 50] about factors such as the unplanned nature of their pregnancy and their experiences of IPV, alongside expectations that they would be judged by their communities for transgress­ ing social norms [34, 40, 49]. Dissonance exacerbated feelings of hopelessness and entrapment [30], already fomented by unplanned pregnancies [34] and IPV [31], and made women less likely to speak to others for help or support.

Women often connected entrapment – a cognitive con­ sequence of emotional distress combined with adverse social circumstances and the need to support young chil­ dren – with suicidal thoughts [30, 35, 40, 44]. Two studies of adolescents [33, 40] described low self-esteem, linked to condemnation by healthcare professionals and their community:

It has to do with how you perceive yourself, [if] he sees me as not good enough then maybe you will find that boyfriend that hits you, [then] he is the one that you want to stay with because you think where else will you find another boyfriend? South Africa [33].

Perinatal mental health impacts of IPV Included studies described a range of emotional impacts of perinatal IPV on women in the African region. Behav­ ioural manifestations included withdrawal from social contact and family activities, including childcare, selfneglect and weight loss or gain [30–32, 34, 35, 37, 38, 43, 50]. Several studies noted that although women identified feelings of tearfulness, stress, irritability, difficulty con­ centrating, forgetfulness, poor sleep, reduced motivation and sometimes spoke of depression, these were largely contextualised in terms of relationship and other stress­ ors [30–32, 38]. In Ethiopia, emotional difficulties were characterised as ‘thinking too much’: anxious, guilty or angry ruminations onlow income, poor health, or marital conflict: [38]

He is always insulting me. That is the case and aggravates my illness … If he makes me free, my mind will be free, but he didn’t make me free; due to this I will stress. Ethiopia [38].

Studies raised persistent physical symptoms, such as dizziness, collapses and fatigue [38], which participants often linked to the ‘stress’ of perinatal IPV [29, 30]. These symptoms were experienced in addition to physi­ cal health problems, including injuries, miscarriages [48], hypertension, chronic pain [50], and avoidance of obstet­ ric care, including unsafe abortion [34, 40].

Several studies reported severe distress, leading women to adopt a fatalistic outlook. Some women reported cop­ ing with distress through spirituality [30, 38, 45], such as prayer, attending holy water sites, or seeing traditional healers. Others focused on the well-being of their chil­ dren, especially where a child had previously died from HIV [46]. Women also reported using substances, con­ sidering or attempting suicide or infanticide [29–31, 34, 35, 38, 49, 50]:

I thought many times about committing suicide. I attempted to kill my daughter many times. Ethiopia [48].

Cycles of suffering In Ethiopia [30] and South Africa [29], women expressed worries about physical harm to the unborn from the stress of IPV, as well as from alcohol consumed to cope with abuse. In one Kenyan study, coping by chewing the stimulant leaf, khat, was normalised and participants were unconcerned about impacting the unborn [39]. Children were impacted by witnessing abuse [47], having to mediate between parents [30], facing their mother’s anger and sadness [29, 31], or acting as her carer [44]. Some children grew hostile towards their mothers, cre­ ating dynamics mimicking parental conflict and violence:

We [my husband and I] could fight until neighbours come to separate us… because of that [fighting] the children don’t respect [me] especially when the man is not at home and when I say something they don’t obey me. Ghana [50].

Two South African studies conducted with antenatal [47], pre- and post-natal women [34] highlighted high rates of community and societal violence in impover­ ished communities with unsafe housing, as harmful to women’s mental health [34]. They linked wider societal normalisation of violence, including against children, to intergenerational cycles of ‘continuous trauma’ [47].

Finally, several studies identified how community responses to IPV inadvertently worsened women’s cir­ cumstances, for example by imposing fines paid from family budgets [49] or imprisoning perpetrators, depriv­ ing women of partner support or income [50]. Ineffec­ tual responses to IPV, such as reinforcement of abuse, inaccessible [50], unaffordable, bureaucratic or corrupt prosecution routes [49], coercion to return, or pres­ sure to accommodate abuse, were common [30]. These experiences were linked to ‘helplessness’ among profes­ sionals [49]. Clinicians also reported limited training or experience of mental health [38] and IPV [30] in Ethio­ pia and Kenya [49]. The lack of a meaningful, harmonised response to IPV served to reinforce women’s sense of hopelessness [30].

Discussion Summary of findings This qualitative meta-synthesis found that despite the high prevalence of perinatal mental health conditions and IPV in the African region, only two published qual­ itative studies had explicitly set out to explore relation­ ships between the two. Among those which did, and


<!-- Page 12 -->


Page 12 of 16 Corkery-Hayward et al. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth          (2026) 26:648

those which identified these relationships as part of wider qualitative exploration, we identified a rich, diverse lit­ erature from a range of countries in the region. Included studies found that socio-cultural norms, perinatal abuse, dependence and vulnerability, and specific foci of distress all interacted to impact perinatal mental health. Across these themes, inter-generational cycles of suffering from abuse and its consequences, proved a pervasive, overarching concern.

Our meta-synthesis aligns with findings of wider qualitative research in Africa, pointing to intersections between poor perinatal mental health and psychoso­ cial adversity. In Zambia, a qualitative study of perina­ tal distress which did not discuss IPV identified links between denial of paternity and financial anxiety, and between partner infidelity and fears of contracting HIV [51]. In Nigeria, a qualitative study of IPV which did not focus on the perinatal period identified children as common reasons for tolerating abusive relationships in the context of entrenched patriarchal norms, espe­ cially around women's financial autonomy [52]. A quali­ tative study of perinatal mental health in Malawi also noted partner infidelity, financial concerns and anxiety about partner reactions to HIV disclosure as stressors [53]. Women in Malawi stressed the central importance of partner support, underscoring our finding that men’s failure to fulfil expectations was a focus of women's dis­ tress. Dependence on partners intersected with other vulnerabilities to perinatal IPV and its mental health consequences. This finding is in line with evidence that epidemics of gender-based violence often interact, in synergistic (syndemic) fashion with other epidemics, of mental ill-health, substance abuse, and HIV infection [54]. Thus, gender-based violence needs to be understood in context, together with its intersections with wider psy­ chosocial adversity [55].

Our findings align with a meta-synthesis of IPV studies enrolling African men, which found that socio-cultural expectations of female obedience, community normalisa­ tion and reinforcement of IPV perpetuated cycles of vio­ lence [56]. Qualitative research in Nigeria found that fear of abandonment was a barrier to women leaving abu­ sive relationships, and exacerbated by patriarchal norms which explicitly or implicitly position women as property [52]. Such fears of being alone can prevent women from disclosing abuse and accessing health and social care services. We found that entrapment left women feeling hopeless, with thoughts of suicide and infanticide com­ monly reported. This finding is supported by evidence that parental mental health conditions are an indepen­ dent risk factor for child maltreatment, with intergen­ erational cycles of abuse and trauma requiring integrated intervention [57].

Adolescents, particularly, described compounded impacts of familial and societal stigma towards preg­ nancy, rejection by social support networks, and loss of educational opportunities [39, 41, 58], in addition to IPV. A study which followed up 8,850 pregnant adult women with 772 pregnant adolescents in Nigeria found that the prevalence of depression at six months postpar­ tum was significantly higher among adolescents (17.7%) than adults (6.9%) [59]. This increased risk of depression is in addition to the elevated baseline prevalence of sui­ cidal thoughts among adolescent females. For example, a global study enrolling over 220,000 adolescents found that those in the African region had the highest preva­ lence of suicidal ideation and suicide planning [60]. In settings of elevated maternal and neonatal mortality, fatalistic outlooks towards IPV, HIV and childbirth are likely to exacerbate hopelessness further [61, 62]. Indeed, perinatal IPV is associated with reduced antenatal care attendance, which can further limit opportunities for intervention [63].

In corroboration with existing literature [21, 64], women in the African region experienced a range of perinatal mental health and somatic symptoms linked to perinatal IPV. These often manifested outside biomedical diagnostic categories, through culturally specific idioms, such as ‘thinking too much’ [38], a symptom previously linked to rumination in Zimbabwe [65] and incorpo­ rated into the ‘Friendship Bench’ model of problem-solv­ ing therapy [66]. Wider research in Africa [67–70] has reported that bodily distress, such as persistent physical symptoms, may be more commonly identified than men­ tal health consequences of IPV. Somatic symptoms may therefore be a particularly salient outcome measure for future research, given systematic review evidence that IPV exposure is associated with chronic pain [71, 72] and functional gastrointestinal symptoms [73].

The degree of somatic symptoms among perinatal women experiencing IPV chimes with evidence sup­ porting mental health benefits of somatic and mindbody interventions for IPV survivors. A meta-analysis of 12 randomized, controlled trials (RCTs) of mind-body therapies for female violence survivors found significant reductions in anxiety, depressive and post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms in the intervention compared to the control group [74]. However, included studies were predominantly conducted in high-income countries and none in the African region. In Uganda, the Move with HaRT (Healing and Resilience after Trauma) group inter­ vention incorporates yogic poses, breathing exercises, mindfulness, and discussions [75]. Following promising preliminary findings in an uncontrolled design [76] and a non-randomised study [75], an RCT is underway with survivors of human trafficking. There is less evidence for


<!-- Page 13 -->


Page 13 of 16 Corkery-Hayward et al. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth          (2026) 26:648

mind-body approaches for the perinatal mental health of IPV survivors in the African region, however.

While spirituality, attending traditional or faith healers and caring for children were common coping strategies [30, 38, 45, 46], included studies less frequently discussed roles antenatal and maternity care can play. Clinicians reported limited training on IPV or perinatal mental health [30, 38], in line with findings that health workers in Ethiopia had limited awareness of non-physical IPV and its harms in pregnancy [77]. Focusing on physical IPV can limit the effectiveness of IPV screening in ante­ natal care, diminishing opportunities to provide sup­ port and make referrals to appropriate services. Variable responses to and services for women experiencing IPV may contribute to healthcare workers’ reticence to screen or intervene, in addition to viewing IPV as outside their clinical remit [78].

In terms of evidence for intervention, an RCT in Rwanda found that a 12 session gender-transformative couples’ programme targeting expectant fathers and fathers of young children reduced IPV, physical punish­ ment of children and men’s engagement with antenatal care [79]. However, a gender-transformative interven­ tion delivered to couples (irrespective of parenthood) in Ethiopia did not find reductions in women’s experiences of IPV [80]. When delivered to men alone, the interven­ tion reduced self-reported IPV perpetration by recipients and male community non-recipients, but not IPV victi­ misation reported by women [81]. Relevant to our find­ ing of perinatal women's concerns about meeting their basic needs, a recent RCT found that a single cash trans­ fer enhanced the impact of group therapy on women's mental health outcomes, but not their experiences of IPV [82]. In addition to illuminating complex processes underlying the mental health impacts of perinatal IPV, qualitative methods are essential for understanding rela­ tionships between contexts, mechanisms and outcomes in which IPV interventions are implemented.

Although ethical review processes can obstruct pub­ lication of gender-based violence research in low- and middle-income countries [], a minority of included stud­ ies described pathways and procedures for safeguard­ ing participants. This highlights the need for continued refinement of ethical research procedures to protect potentially vulnerable participants experiencing IPV and perinatal mental health conditions [84].

Limitations Restricting our search to English-language publica­ tions in peer-reviewed literature means that we may not have identified all potentially relevant evidence. Selfreporting of IPV and mental health in all studies meant that in the context of entrenched patriarchal norms and

stigmatization of mental health conditions, some wom­ en’s experiences are likely to have been missed.

All included studies reported quotations in English, even when conducted in local dialects. Translation pro­ cesses can lose rich, culturally relevant findings and con­ text, especially when no direct translations for cultural idioms exist. Expanding this review to the grey literature might capture mental health impacts of perinatal IPV not adequately represented in peer reviewed English-lan­ guage literature.

Recommendations and future research Our qualitative meta-synthesis highlights the need to investigate and address intersecting factors that shape women’s perinatal mental health and develop multisec­ toral responses to IPV and related adversities, tailored for the needs of women in the African region. Given the range of psychological and somatic symptoms associated with perinatal IPV, maternity care represents an impor­ tant point of contact for identifying and responding to IPV, mental health and related harms [85]. Gaps in ANC provider training, supervision, resources and referral pathways highlight key areas for intervention.

Investment in health systems which support women during the perinatal period, including community, inpa­ tient, social support and faith-based services, could strengthen culturally appropriate responses. Future research should explore women’s experiences of health­ care interactions when seeking support for mental health consequences of perinatal IPV, with a focus on those with intersecting marginalities. For example, stigmatisation and hostility from healthcare professionals towards ado­ lescent participants may impede healthcare access and help-seeking, worsening mental health outcomes. Quali­ tative research exploring these dynamics could inform more person-centred models of care.

However, the current period of major retrenchment [86] of global health research and aid funding places such critical initiatives at risk. Multisectoral responses target­ ing multifacted drivers of perinatal IPV across socio-eco­ logical levels require sustained funding and government support to address their root causes and prevent associ­ ated long-term harms to women and children's health and safety.

https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02143-3 Article Health effects associated with exposure of children to physical violence, psychological violence and neglect: a Burden of Proof study

The health toll of child maltreatment or violence against children (VAC) has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. Here, in our systematic review and meta-analyses, we focused on the health impacts of physical violence, psychological violence and neglect during childhood. Utilizing the Burden of Proof methodology, which generates conservative measures of association while accounting for heterogeneity between input studies, we evaluated 35 associations between VAC and adverse health outcomes, identifying 27 statistically significant links. The associations between physical violence and major depressive disorder, ischaemic heart disease, alcohol use disorder, eating disorders and drug use disorders were rated as moderately weak, reflecting a small effect size and/or inconsistent evidence. The minimum increased risk ranged from 16% for depression to 2% for drug use disorders. Psychological violence showed similar moderately weak associations with drug use disorders (8% minimum risk increase), migraine (7%) and gynaecological diseases (2%). Neglect was linked to at least a 15% increased risk for anxiety disorders. The other 18 associations were weaker due to smaller effect sizes and/or less consistent evidence. Despite the limitations of the existing evidence, our analysis highlights substantial health impacts for VAC survivors, underscoring the need for health system prioritization and continued efforts to eliminate all forms of VAC.

The safeguarding of children against all forms of violence is a fundamental right enshrined in the Convention on the Rights of the Child, alongside other international human rights treaties. Yet, exposure to violence continues to be a harsh reality for children across the world, transcending economic and social status, culture, religion and ethnicity1. Worldwide, nearly 1 billion children aged 2–17 years are subjected to physical, sexual or emotional violence or neglect each year2, with three in four young children experiencing physical punishment or psychological aggression on a regular basis3. The most dangerous spaces for children are too often those that are supposed to be safe environments, most notably the home, where parents, relatives and those who are supposed to provide care are frequently the perpetrators4.

Experiencing and witnessing violence, especially at an early age, can have profound and far-reaching consequences on immediate and long-term well-being. Beyond deaths5, violence against children (VAC), represented by forms of direct abuse or neglect of children, has been linked to a spectrum of adverse health outcomes, including physical injuries, developmental issues, chronic diseases, childhood pregnancy and a range of mental health conditions6–13. Early-life exposure to violence also increases the likelihood of high-risk coping behaviours14,15, certain unsafe sexual practices16 and substance use17, which exacerbate negative health outcomes associated with experiencing violence as a child. The societal impact of VAC is equally substantial, undermining educational attainment and diminishing economic potential18,19. Compounding this, exposure to VAC is associated with subsequent

Such efforts are essential in amplifying the urgency for global attention and positioning VAC appropriately in policy and budgeting agendas. In this study, drawing from a systematic review conducted as part of an initiative by the Lancet Commission on Gender-Based Violence and Maltreatment of Young People to quantify the health burden of violence across the lifespan, we estimated the associations between childhood physical violence, psychological violence and neglect and a diverse set of health outcomes. The health risks associated with CSA are reported in a prior publication10. For this purpose, we used the Burden of Proof methodology developed by Zheng and colleagues29, which yields a conservative estimate of the harmful effects of exposure to VAC, rigorously quantifies the consistency of the underlying evidence and translates the findings into an easily interpretable star rating system, where one star denotes a weak association and/or inconsistent evidence and five stars indicate a strong association supported by consistent evidence. This analytical framework incorporates—among other systematic modelling components—covariate selection and adjustment to account for known variation in input study characteristics and further quantifies remaining ‘unexplained’ between-study heterogeneity (that is, gamma and its uncertainty) using random effects modelling. Therefore, this method more fully accounts for heterogeneity compared with traditional meta-analytic approaches, providing uniquely robust, credible and well-specified evidence for policymakers and public health professionals dedicated to reducing VAC and its impacts. Although existing estimates of prevalence suggest that the magnitude of the problem is massive, they are probably underestimates of the true extent of VAC, owing to the inherent challenges in accurately assessing the full spectrum of VAC and the likelihood of underreporting due to stigma and fear of reprisal22,23. Further, some forms of VAC (for example, corporal punishment) are socially accepted, tacitly condoned or not perceived as being abusive in certain settings, which both normalizes what is a public health risk and fuels a dangerous misconception that VAC remains a marginal and rare phenomenon. The burden of disease associated with VAC has also been underestimated so far. The 2021 iteration of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) estimates that childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is responsible for 2.8 million disability-adjusted life years (a measure of both premature death and years lived in ill health) globally24. However, this estimate is based on the association of CSA with a limited number of health outcomes and, hence, underestimates disability-adjusted life years. Further, GBD does not yet account for the loss of health resulting from other types of VAC beyond CSA. These limitations extend beyond the GBD. Most systematic reviews concentrate on the health impacts of adverse childhood experiences as an umbrella term, failing to disentangle the health consequences associated with specific forms of VAC25,26. Moreover, these reviews are frequently restricted in the range of health outcomes investigated, with many focusing primarily on reproductive outcomes among women or mental and substance use disorders26–28. Background VAC is a critical human rights and public health issue, with nearly one billion children experiencing physical, sexual or psychological abuse or neglect annually. VAC, also referred to as child maltreatment, leads to severe health, developmental and psychosocial consequences, fostering cycles of violence that impact future generations. Yet, the full scale of the crisis is probably underestimated due to challenges quantifying exposure to violence and societal normalization of some abusive behaviours. Here, we systematically reviewed the published literature across seven databases and conducted meta-analyses to assess the health impacts of childhood physical violence, psychological violence and neglect on a diverse range of health outcomes.

Main findings and limitations We quantified the associations of childhood physical violence, psychological violence and neglect with 15, 11 and 9 specific health outcomes, respectively. Out of the 35 risk–outcome pairs evaluated, our results suggest statistically significant increased risk for 11 health outcomes in individuals who experienced physical violence as a child, 10 in those subjected to childhood psychological violence and 6 in those who were neglected during childhood. Using conservative Burden of Proof metrics that account for between-study heterogeneity and quantify both the effect size for the association and the strength of the underlying evidence, estimated associations ranged from moderately weak (two stars) for 9 risk–outcome pairs to weak (one star) for 18 pairs. Our conservative interpretation of the data suggests that exposure to physical violence increases the risk of major depressive disorder and ischaemic heart disease by at least 16% and 15%, respectively. Psychological violence exposure increases the risk of drug use disorders by at least 8% and the risk of migraine by at least 7%, while childhood neglect increases anxiety disorders risk by a minimum of 15%. One-star risk–outcome pairs primarily reflect a lack of available data coupled with considerable heterogeneity in the data that are available, suggesting more research is needed. Our study was limited by several factors, including variability in how violence exposure was defined across the included studies, which contributes to between-study heterogeneity. Although some discrepancies could be addressed through bias covariates, others may have also affected our results. In addition, treating physical violence, psychological violence and neglect as separate, dichotomous risk factors may oversimplify the complexities of these exposures and their associated health risks, which can be interrelated and vary with severity or frequency. Our analysis was limited to health outcomes that align with the Global Burden of Disease definitions and were supported by at least three published studies. Potential health risks from other forms of VAC or outcomes not covered by the present meta-analysis may represent further unaddressed aspects of the total health burden of exposure to VAC.

Policy implications In light of the profound health impacts of childhood physical violence, psychological violence and neglect revealed by our systematic review, it is critical for policymakers, health professionals and advocates to urgently prioritize the elimination of all forms of VAC. The evidence calls for a comprehensive approach that synthesizes public health policies, socioeconomic strategies and educational initiatives to prevent exposure to violence and to support those who have survived it. With the aspiration to meet the Sustainable Development Goal of eradicating all forms of VAC by 2030, prevention and response measures must be inclusive, ensuring that no child is left behind. This pursuit is not just a moral obligation; it is also a prudent investment towards securing healthier, violence-free futures for upcoming generations. To propel this mission forward, enhancing data collection on the various dimensions of violence and its consequences is imperative to provide the foundation for a global health agenda that prioritizes children’s welfare. By committing to adversity-free childhoods and implementing evidence-based interventions that preempt both childhood abuse and its potential continuation into adulthood, we can dismantle the cycle of violence and establish a legacy of health and prosperity that benefits all individuals and societies.

Results A total of 75,331 records were screened as part of an initial systematic review of the literature, which included articles in any language indexed across seven databases over the 54 years between 1 January 1970 and 31 January 2024. Of these records, 638 studies that reported on the association between exposure to any type of violence during childhood or gender-based violence (GBV) and specific health-related outcomes met the predefined eligibility criteria (Methods). All other studies were found to be ineligible, including 452 with an ineligible study design (Fig. 1). While the initial review encompassed literature reporting on any form of violence, the current analysis was narrowed to focus on the health effects of physical violence, psychological violence or neglect occurring before the age of 18, regardless of the perpetrator of the abuse. In alignment with the International Classification of Violence against Children (ICVAC)30, established by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), these forms of violence respectively refer to deliberate, unwanted and non-essential acts of physical violence; verbal or non-verbal psychological violence; and physical, emotional, medical or educational neglect (Supplementary Table 1). A summary

list of VAC definitions used in the underlying studies is presented in Supplementary Table 2. Based on the above criteria, we included 111 unique studies (Supplementary Table 3)—the majority being prospective cohorts (n = 69) and from high-income nations (n = 89)—from which we leveraged relevant data for those risk–outcome pairs with at least 3 studies reporting on an outcome definition consistent with the case definitions used for GBD causes (Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). These studies formed the basis for assessing 15 eligible health outcomes potentially associated with childhood physical violence (94 studies), 11 outcomes related to psychological violence (55 studies) and 9 outcomes connected to neglect (50 studies). The most frequently investigated health consequences across the various forms of VAC included mental health conditions, such as major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders; substance use disorders, such as alcohol use disorders and drug use disorders; followed by diabetes mellitus type 2, asthma, self-harm and schizophrenia (Table 2). We also report a Burden of Proof Risk Function (BPRF) value and corresponding Risk–Outcome Score (ROS) and star rating for each pair. The BPRF (equivalent to the fifth percentile of RR draws closest to null) complements the mean RR function and, by design, reflects the lowest reasonable estimate of the effect of the violence exposure on the health outcome of interest, based on the currently available evidence. The conservative BPRF is converted into a ROS, with higher, more positive ROS values indicating a greater harmful effect supported by strong underlying evidence. These ROS values are translated into corresponding increasing star ratings, ranging from 1 to 5, to simplify the interpretation of results29. Pooled RR and star ratings for each risk–outcome are also displayed in Fig. 2 for ease of comparison across forms of violence and health outcomes.

Physical violence exposure Among the 15 analysed health outcomes, mental health and substance use disorders made up the bulk of the 5 outcomes with the highest-rated (2 stars; ROS between the 0.00 and 0.14 predefined thresholds29) associations with exposure to physical VAC. Twenty-six studies31–56 examined the association between childhood physical violence and major depressive disorder (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 3). We conservatively estimated that those who experienced physical violence as a child have at least a 16% higher risk of major depressive disorder compared with their unexposed counterparts (BPRF 1.16). The star rating of two indicates moderately weak evidence of an association, due to either or both a small effect size and lack of consistent evidence (Table 2). Similarly, the association of physical violence during childhood with alcohol use disorders48,57–63, eating disorders45,53,64,65 and drug use disorders57,59,60,62,63,66–71 were also rated as moderately weak (two

stars), with a minimum increase in risk of 4% (BPRF 1.04), 4% (BPRF 1.04) and 2% (BPRF 1.02), respectively, for each of these outcomes in people who experienced physical violence as a child (Table 2). Our findings across these outcomes are largely, but not entirely, consistent regardless of model parameters and data point restrictions tested in various sensitivity analyses (Extended Data Fig. 1, Supplementary Tables 6–9 and Supplementary Figs. 1–7). Among the most notable differences, we identified a three-star association between childhood physical violence and alcohol use disorders when the outcome definition was restricted to clinical alcohol dependence instead of also including measures of alcohol abuse (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 8). Other than mental health and substance use disorders, ischaemic heart disease (IHD)58,72–74 accounted for the remaining two-star association with childhood physical violence. We estimated a 15% minimum increase in the risk of this condition for individuals exposed to physical violence in childhood (BPRF = 1.15). The association was reduced to a one-star rating when including only effect sizes that examined physical violence committed by an unspecified or unrestricted perpetrator (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 10). Anxiety disorders31,35,40,43,47,51,56,75–78 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 11) was the only mental health condition among the six outcomes with one-star associations with childhood physical violence (Table 2). While we identified sufficient evidence of an association for this risk–outcome pair, the evidence was rated as weak. The star rating for this association changed to two stars when excluding studies that only consisted of post-traumatic stress disorder in their outcome definitions and when excluding perpetrator-specific violence exposures (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 11). Similarly, we found weak one-star evidence of associations with childhood physical violence for type 2 diabetes41,58,74,79–87, migraine58,88–90, self-harm37,40,48,53,91–102, asthma58,81,103–106 and gynaecological diseases107–112.
